questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: At a specific instant, the magnitudes of the position, velocity, and acceleration of a particle undergoing simple harmonic motion are observed to be $2 \text{ cm}$, $1 \text{ m/s}$, and $10 \text{ m/s}^2$, respectively. Determine the amplitude and the time period of the motion.
questions.solution:
Given $x = 2 \text{ cm} = 0.02 \text{ m}$, $v = 1 \text{ m/s}$, and $a = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$.

In simple harmonic motion, the magnitude of acceleration is given by $a = \omega^2 x$.

Substituting the given values:

$10 = \omega^2 \times 0.02$

$\omega^2 = \dfrac{10}{0.02} = 500 \text{ rad}^2/\text{s}^2$

$\omega = \sqrt{500} = 10\sqrt{5} \text{ rad/s}$

The time period $T$ is given by:

$T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega} = \dfrac{2\pi}{10\sqrt{5}} \approx \dfrac{2 \times 3.14}{22.36} \approx 0.28 \text{ s}$

The velocity in SHM is given by $v = \omega \sqrt{A^2 - x^2}$.

Squaring both sides:

$v^2 = \omega^2 (A^2 - x^2)$

Substituting the known values:

$1^2 = 500 (A^2 - 0.02^2)$

$1 = 500 (A^2 - 0.0004)$

$A^2 - 0.0004 = \dfrac{1}{500} = 0.002$

$A^2 = 0.002 + 0.0004 = 0.0024 \text{ m}^2$

$A = \sqrt{0.0024} \text{ m} = \sqrt{24} \times 10^{-2} \text{ m} = \sqrt{24} \text{ cm}$

Since $\sqrt{24} \approx 4.899$, the amplitude is $A \approx 4.9 \text{ cm}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: For a particle executing simple harmonic motion, the maximum speed and acceleration are $10 \text{ cm/s}$ and $50 \text{ cm/s}^2$, respectively. Determine the position(s) of the particle when its speed is $8 \text{ cm/s}$.
questions.solution:
Given $v_{\text{max}} = A\omega = 10 \text{ cm/s}$ and $a_{\text{max}} = A\omega^2 = 50 \text{ cm/s}^2$.

Dividing the two expressions, we get:

$\omega = \dfrac{A\omega^2}{A\omega} = \dfrac{50}{10} = 5 \text{ rad/s}$

The amplitude $A$ is:

$A = \dfrac{10}{\omega} = \dfrac{10}{5} = 2 \text{ cm}$

The velocity $v$ of a particle in SHM at a distance $x$ from the mean position is given by:

$v = \omega \sqrt{A^2 - x^2}$

Substituting $v = 8 \text{ cm/s}$, $\omega = 5 \text{ rad/s}$, and $A = 2 \text{ cm}$:

$8 = 5 \sqrt{2^2 - x^2}$

Squaring both sides:

$64 = 25(4 - x^2)$

$25x^2 = 100 - 64 = 36$

$x^2 = \dfrac{36}{25} = 1.44$

$x = \pm 1.2 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle having a mass of $10 \text{ g}$ oscillates according to the equation $x = (2.0 \text{ cm}) \sin[(100 \text{ s}^{-1}) t + \pi/6]$. Determine the amplitude, the time period, and the spring constant for this motion.
questions.solution:
Comparing the given equation $x = (2.0 \text{ cm}) \sin[(100 \text{ s}^{-1}) t + \pi/6]$ with the standard equation of SHM $x = A \sin(\omega t + \phi)$, we get:

Amplitude $A = 2.0 \text{ cm}$

Angular frequency $\omega = 100 \text{ rad/s}$

Time period $T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega} = \dfrac{2\pi}{100} \approx 0.063 \text{ s}$

Spring constant $k = m\omega^2 = (10 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg})(100 \text{ rad/s})^2 = 100 \text{ N/m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle undergoes simple harmonic motion having an amplitude of $10 \text{ cm}$. At what distance from the mean position will its kinetic and potential energies be equal?
questions.solution:
Let the distance from the mean position be $x$.

The kinetic energy of a particle in SHM is given by $K = \dfrac{1}{2} m \omega^2 (A^2 - x^2)$.

The potential energy is given by $U = \dfrac{1}{2} m \omega^2 x^2$.

Given that kinetic and potential energies are equal, $K = U$.

$\dfrac{1}{2} m \omega^2 (A^2 - x^2) = \dfrac{1}{2} m \omega^2 x^2$

$A^2 - x^2 = x^2$

$2x^2 = A^2$

$x = \dfrac{A}{\sqrt{2}}$

Substituting the amplitude $A = 10 \text{ cm}$:

$x = \dfrac{10}{\sqrt{2}} = 5\sqrt{2} \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle executes simple harmonic motion with an amplitude of $10 \text{ cm}$ and a time period of $6 \text{ s}$. At $t = 0$, it is located at $x = 5 \text{ cm}$ and is moving towards the positive x-direction. Determine the equation for the displacement $x$ as a function of time $t$, and calculate the magnitude of the particle's acceleration at $t = 4 \text{ s}$.
questions.solution:
The angular frequency of the particle is $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T} = \dfrac{2\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{3} \text{ rad/s}$.

The general equation for displacement in SHM is $x(t) = A \sin(\omega t + \phi_0)$.

Given $A = 10 \text{ cm}$, and at $t = 0$, $x = 5 \text{ cm}$:

$10 \sin(\phi_0) = 5 \Rightarrow \sin(\phi_0) = \dfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \phi_0 = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ or $\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$.

The velocity is $v(t) = A\omega \cos(\omega t + \phi_0)$. Since the particle is moving towards the positive x-direction at $t = 0$, $v(0) > 0$, which implies $\cos(\phi_0) > 0$.

Therefore, $\phi_0 = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

The equation for displacement is $x(t) = 10 \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}t + \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \text{ cm}$.

At $t = 4 \text{ s}$, the displacement is:

$x(4) = 10 \sin\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3} + \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = 10 \sin\left(\dfrac{9\pi}{6}\right) = 10 \sin\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) = -10 \text{ cm}$.

The magnitude of acceleration is $|a| = \omega^2 |x|$:

$|a| = \left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)^2 \times 10 = \dfrac{10\pi^2}{9}$

Taking $\pi^2 \approx 9.87$, we get $|a| \approx \dfrac{98.7}{9} \approx 11 \text{ cm/s}^2$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle having a mass of $10 \text{ g}$ oscillates according to the equation $x = (2.0 \text{ cm}) \sin[(100 \text{ s}^{-1}) t + \pi/6]$. Determine the position, the velocity, and the acceleration of the particle at $t = 0$.
questions.solution:
The given equation of motion is $x = 2.0 \sin(100t + \pi/6) \text{ cm}$.

At $t = 0$, the position is:
$x = 2.0 \sin(\pi/6) = 2.0 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 1.0 \text{ cm}$

The velocity is the rate of change of position:
$v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = \dfrac{d}{dt} [2.0 \sin(100t + \pi/6)] = 200 \cos(100t + \pi/6) \text{ cm/s}$

At $t = 0$, the velocity is:
$v = 200 \cos(\pi/6) = 200 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 100\sqrt{3} \text{ cm/s} = \sqrt{3} \text{ m/s} \approx 1.73 \text{ m/s}$

The acceleration is the rate of change of velocity:
$a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{d}{dt} [200 \cos(100t + \pi/6)] = -20000 \sin(100t + \pi/6) \text{ cm/s}^2$

At $t = 0$, the acceleration is:
$a = -20000 \sin(\pi/6) = -20000 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = -10000 \text{ cm/s}^2 = -100 \text{ m/s}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle begins its motion at $t = 0$ according to the equation $x = 5 \sin(20 t + \pi/3)$, where $x$ is in centimetre and $t$ is in second. At what time will the particle first have zero acceleration?
questions.solution:
The equation of motion of the particle is given by:

$x = 5 \sin(20 t + \dfrac{\pi}{3})$

The velocity $v$ is the first derivative of displacement with respect to time:

$v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 100 \cos(20 t + \dfrac{\pi}{3})$

The acceleration $a$ is the first derivative of velocity with respect to time:

$a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = -2000 \sin(20 t + \dfrac{\pi}{3})$

For the acceleration to be zero, we must have:

$-2000 \sin(20 t + \dfrac{\pi}{3}) = 0$

$\sin(20 t + \dfrac{\pi}{3}) = 0$

This implies that the phase must be an integer multiple of $\pi$. Since we need the first time $t > 0$ when acceleration is zero, we equate the phase to the next multiple of $\pi$ after $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, which is $\pi$:

$20 t + \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \pi$

$20 t = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$

$t = \dfrac{2\pi}{60} = \dfrac{\pi}{30} \text{ s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle starts moving at $t = 0$ with its position given by the equation $x = 5 \sin(20 t + \pi/3)$, where $x$ is in centimetre and $t$ is in second. Determine the time when the particle first comes to rest.
questions.solution:
Given the position of the particle as $x = 5 \sin\left(20t + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$.

The velocity of the particle is the rate of change of position with respect to time:

$v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = \dfrac{d}{dt} \left[ 5 \sin\left(20t + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \right]$

$v = 100 \cos\left(20t + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$

The particle comes to rest when its velocity becomes zero. Thus, $v = 0$.

$100 \cos\left(20t + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 0$

$\cos\left(20t + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 0$

For the first time the particle comes to rest, the phase angle must be equal to $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

$20t + \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

$20t = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{3}$

$20t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$

$t = \dfrac{\pi}{120} \text{ s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle starts its motion at $t = 0$ and its position is given by the equation $x = 5 \sin(20 t + \pi/3)$, where $x$ is in centimetre and $t$ is in second. Find the time at which the particle first attains maximum speed.
questions.solution:
Given the position of the particle:

$x = 5 \sin(20 t + \pi/3)$

The velocity of the particle is the rate of change of position:

$v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 100 \cos(20 t + \pi/3)$

The speed of the particle is maximum when it passes through the mean position ($x = 0$), which corresponds to $|v|$ being maximum, or $|\cos(20 t + \pi/3)| = 1$.

This condition is satisfied when:

$20 t + \dfrac{\pi}{3} = n\pi$

For the first time after $t = 0$, we set $n = 1$:

$20 t + \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \pi$

$20 t = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$

$t = \dfrac{2\pi}{60} = \dfrac{\pi}{30} \text{ s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle travels in simple harmonic motion described by the equation $x = 2.0 \cos(50 \pi t + \tan^{-1} 0.75)$, where $x$ is in centimetres and $t$ is in seconds. The motion is initiated at $t = 0$. At what time does the particle come to rest for the first time?
questions.solution:
The position of the particle is given by:

$x = 2.0 \cos(50 \pi t + \tan^{-1} 0.75)$

The velocity of the particle is the rate of change of position:

$v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = -100 \pi \sin(50 \pi t + \tan^{-1} 0.75)$

The particle comes to rest when its velocity is zero, i.e., $v = 0$:

$\sin(50 \pi t + \tan^{-1} 0.75) = 0$

For the particle to come to rest for the first time after $t = 0$, the phase must be equal to $\pi$ (since the initial phase $\tan^{-1} 0.75$ is between $0$ and $\pi/2$):

$50 \pi t + \tan^{-1} 0.75 = \pi$

We know that $\tan^{-1} 0.75 = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right) \approx 37^{\circ}$.

Converting $37^{\circ}$ to radians:

$\tan^{-1} 0.75 \approx \dfrac{37 \pi}{180}$

Substituting this into the phase equation:

$50 \pi t + \dfrac{37 \pi}{180} \approx \pi$

Dividing the entire equation by $\pi$:

$50 t + \dfrac{37}{180} = 1$

$50 t = 1 - \dfrac{37}{180} = \dfrac{143}{180}$

$t = \dfrac{143}{180 \times 50} = \dfrac{143}{9000} \approx 0.01588 \text{ s}$

Rounding to two significant figures, we get:

$t \approx 1.6 \times 10^{-2} \text{ s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle travels in simple harmonic motion described by the equation $x = 2.0 \cos(50 \pi t + \tan^{-1} 0.75)$, where $x$ is in centimetres and $t$ is in seconds. The motion is initiated at $t = 0$. At what time does the acceleration attain its maximum magnitude for the first time?
questions.solution:
The displacement of the particle is given by $x = 2.0 \cos(50 \pi t + \tan^{-1} 0.75)$.

The acceleration of a particle in simple harmonic motion is $a = -\omega^2 x$. The magnitude of acceleration is maximum when the displacement is at its extreme positions, i.e., $x = \pm 2.0$.

This condition is satisfied when $\cos(50 \pi t + \tan^{-1} 0.75) = \pm 1$.

Let $\phi = \tan^{-1}(0.75) = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)$. The angle $\phi$ is approximately $37^{\circ}$ or $\dfrac{37\pi}{180}$ radians.

At $t = 0$, the phase is $\phi \approx 37^{\circ}$. The first time the magnitude of acceleration reaches its maximum is when the phase equals $\pi$ (or $180^{\circ}$).

Equating the phase to $\pi$:

$50 \pi t + \phi = \pi$

$50 \pi t = \pi - \phi$

Converting to degrees for simpler calculation:

$50 \times 180^{\circ} \times t = 180^{\circ} - 37^{\circ}$

$9000 t = 143$

$t = \dfrac{143}{9000} \approx 0.01588 \text{ s}$

Rounding to appropriate significant figures, we get $t \approx 1.6 \times 10^{-2} \text{ s}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle travels in simple harmonic motion described by the equation $x = 2.0 \cos(50 \pi t + \tan^{-1} 0.75)$, where $x$ is in centimetres and $t$ is in seconds. The motion is initiated at $t = 0$. At what time does the particle come to rest for the second time?
questions.solution:
The given equation of simple harmonic motion is $x = 2.0 \cos(50 \pi t + \phi)$, where $\phi = \tan^{-1}(0.75)$.

The particle comes to rest when its velocity is zero:

$v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = -100 \pi \sin(50 \pi t + \phi) = 0$

This implies $\sin(50 \pi t + \phi) = 0$, which gives $50 \pi t + \phi = n\pi$ for $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$

For the particle to come to rest for the second time, we set $n = 2$:

$50 \pi t + \phi = 2\pi$

$t = \dfrac{2\pi - \phi}{50 \pi} = \dfrac{2}{50} - \dfrac{\phi}{50 \pi}$

Since $\tan \phi = 0.75 = \dfrac{3}{4}$, the angle $\phi \approx 37^\circ$. Converting to radians, $\phi \approx \dfrac{37\pi}{180} \approx 0.205\pi$.

Substituting this value:

$t \approx \dfrac{2\pi - 0.205\pi}{50 \pi} = \dfrac{1.795}{50} = 0.0359 \text{ s}$

Rounding to two significant figures, we get $t \approx 3.6 \times 10^{-2} \text{ s}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: For a simple harmonic motion with a time period $T$, determine the time required for the displacement to increase from half the amplitude to the full amplitude.
questions.solution:
Let the equation of simple harmonic motion starting from the mean position be $x = A \sin(\omega t)$.

Time taken to reach $x = A/2$ from the mean position is $t_1$:

$\dfrac{A}{2} = A \sin(\omega t_1) \Rightarrow \sin(\omega t_1) = \dfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \omega t_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$

$t_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{6\omega} = \dfrac{\pi}{6} \times \dfrac{T}{2\pi} = \dfrac{T}{12}$

Time taken to reach $x = A$ from the mean position is $t_2$:

$A = A \sin(\omega t_2) \Rightarrow \sin(\omega t_2) = 1 \Rightarrow \omega t_2 = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

$t_2 = \dfrac{\pi}{2\omega} = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \times \dfrac{T}{2\pi} = \dfrac{T}{4}$

Time required to increase the displacement from half the amplitude to the full amplitude is:

$\Delta t = t_2 - t_1 = \dfrac{T}{4} - \dfrac{T}{12} = \dfrac{3T - T}{12} = \dfrac{2T}{12} = \dfrac{T}{6}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A clock's pendulum is replaced by a spring-mass system featuring a spring with a spring constant of $0.1 \text{ N/m}$. Determine the mass that should be attached to the spring.
questions.solution:
The time period of a standard clock pendulum (seconds pendulum) is $T = 2 \text{ s}$.

The time period of a spring-mass system is given by $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$.

Equating the two time periods:

$2 = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{0.1}}$

$1 = \pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{0.1}}$

Squaring both sides and using the approximation $\pi^2 \approx 10$:

$1 = 10 \left(\dfrac{m}{0.1}\right)$

$1 = 100 m$

$m = \dfrac{1}{100} \text{ kg}$

$m = 0.01 \text{ kg} = 10 \text{ g}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block suspended from a vertical spring is in equilibrium, producing an extension $x$ in the spring. Determine the length of an equivalent simple pendulum (i.e., a pendulum having the same frequency as that of the block).
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the block be $m$ and the spring constant be $k$.

In equilibrium, the spring force balances the weight of the block:

$kx = mg \Rightarrow \dfrac{m}{k} = \dfrac{x}{g}$

The time period of oscillation for the block-spring system is given by:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$

Substituting the value of $\dfrac{m}{k}$, we get:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{x}{g}}$

The time period of a simple pendulum of length $L$ is given by:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}$

Since the frequencies (and hence time periods) are equal, we equate the two expressions:

$2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{x}{g}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}$

Squaring both sides, we obtain:

$L = x$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Suspended from a vertical spring, a block of mass $0.5 \text{ kg}$ undergoes simple harmonic motion with an amplitude of $0.1 \text{ m}$ and a time period of $0.314 \text{ s}$. Determine the maximum force exerted by the spring on the block.
questions.solution:
Angular frequency $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T} = \dfrac{2 \times 3.14}{0.314} = 20 \text{ rad/s}$

Maximum acceleration of the block during SHM is $a_{max} = \omega^2 A = (20)^2 \times 0.1 = 40 \text{ m/s}^2$

The maximum force exerted by the spring occurs at the lowest point of the oscillation where the spring is maximally stretched and the acceleration is directed upwards.

Using Newton's second law at the lowest point:

$F_{max} - mg = m a_{max}$

$F_{max} = m(g + a_{max})$

Taking $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$F_{max} = 0.5 \times (10 + 40) = 0.5 \times 50 = 25 \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body of mass $2 \text{ kg}$ suspended from a vertical spring undergoes simple harmonic motion with a period of $4 \text{ s}$. If the oscillations are halted and the body hangs in equilibrium, determine the potential energy stored in the spring.
questions.solution:
The time period of the spring-mass system is given by $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$.

Substituting the given values:

$4 = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{k}}$

Squaring both sides:

$16 = 4\pi^2 \left(\dfrac{2}{k}\right)$

$k = \dfrac{8\pi^2}{16} = \dfrac{\pi^2}{2} \text{ N/m}$

Taking $\pi^2 \approx 10$, we get $k = 5 \text{ N/m}$.

At equilibrium, the spring force balances the weight of the body:

$kx = mg$

$x = \dfrac{mg}{k} = \dfrac{2 \times 10}{5} = 4 \text{ m}$

The potential energy stored in the spring at equilibrium is:

$U = \dfrac{1}{2}kx^2$

$U = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times (4)^2 = 40 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When stretched by $25 \text{ cm}$, a spring stores $5 \text{ J}$ of energy. It is positioned vertically with its lower end fixed. A block secured to the opposite end is made to undergo small oscillations. If the block completes $5$ oscillations each second, determine the mass of the block. (Assume $\pi^2 \approx 10$)
questions.solution:
The potential energy stored in the spring is given by $U = \dfrac{1}{2}kx^2$.

Substituting the given values, $U = 5 \text{ J}$ and $x = 25 \text{ cm} = 0.25 \text{ m}$:

$5 = \dfrac{1}{2} k (0.25)^2$

$5 = \dfrac{1}{2} k \left(\dfrac{1}{16}\right)$

$k = 5 \times 32 = 160 \text{ N/m}$

The frequency of oscillation is $f = 5 \text{ Hz}$. The angular frequency is $\omega = 2\pi f = 10\pi \text{ rad/s}$.

Using the formula for angular frequency $\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}}$:

$\omega^2 = \dfrac{k}{m}$

$(10\pi)^2 = \dfrac{160}{m}$

$100\pi^2 = \dfrac{160}{m}$

Given $\pi^2 \approx 10$:

$1000 = \dfrac{160}{m}$

$m = \dfrac{160}{1000} = 0.16 \text{ kg}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A small block of mass $m$ is placed on a bigger block of mass $M$ that is attached to a vertical spring of spring constant $k$. The system oscillates vertically. Determine the maximum amplitude with which the two blocks can oscillate together without losing contact.
questions.solution:
Let the amplitude of oscillation be $A$.

The angular frequency of the spring-mass system is given by $\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{M+m}}$.

The maximum downward acceleration of the system occurs at the highest point of oscillation and its magnitude is $a_{\max} = \omega^2 A = \dfrac{k}{M+m}A$.

Consider the forces acting on the small block of mass $m$ at the highest point: the downward gravitational force $mg$ and the upward normal reaction $N$ from the bigger block.

The equation of motion for the small block is:
$mg - N = m a_{\max}$

For the block of mass $m$ to not lose contact with the block of mass $M$, the normal reaction must be non-negative ($N \ge 0$).

$mg - m a_{\max} \ge 0$
$\Rightarrow a_{\max} \le g$

Substituting the value of $a_{\max}$:
$\dfrac{k}{M+m}A \le g$
$\Rightarrow A \le \dfrac{(M+m)g}{k}$

Thus, the maximum amplitude with which the two blocks can oscillate together is $\dfrac{(M+m)g}{k}$.
questions.question: A small block of mass $m$ is placed on a bigger block of mass $M$ that is attached to a vertical spring of spring constant $k$. The system oscillates vertically. Determine the maximum amplitude with which the two blocks can oscillate together without losing contact.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A small block of mass $m$ is placed on a bigger block of mass $M$ that is attached to a vertical spring of spring constant $k$. The system oscillates vertically. Find the normal force on the smaller block when it is displaced by a distance $x$ above its equilibrium position. Also, identify when this force is smallest in magnitude.
questions.solution:
Let the upward direction be taken as positive.

When the system is displaced by a distance $x$ above its equilibrium position, the restoring force acting on the combined mass $(M+m)$ is given by:
$F = -kx$

The acceleration of the system is:
$a = \dfrac{F}{M+m} = -\dfrac{kx}{M+m}$

Considering the free body diagram of the smaller block of mass $m$, the forces acting on it are the normal force $N$ upwards and its weight $mg$ downwards. Applying Newton's second law for the smaller block:
$N - mg = ma$

Substituting the expression for acceleration $a$:
$N = m(g + a)$
$N = m\left(g - \dfrac{kx}{M+m}\right)$
$N = mg - \dfrac{mkx}{M+m}$

To find when the normal force is smallest in magnitude, the term subtracted from $mg$ must be as large as possible. This occurs when the upward displacement $x$ is maximum.

The maximum positive displacement $x$ corresponds to the highest point of the oscillation. Therefore, the normal force is smallest at the highest point.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: As illustrated in the figure, a block of mass $m_1$ is fastened to a spring on an incline of angle $\theta$, and a block of mass $m_2$ is placed against it. Determine the compression of the spring when the system is in its equilibrium position.
questions.solution:
Consider the blocks $m_1$ and $m_2$ as a single system of mass $(m_1 + m_2)$.

In the equilibrium position, the net force acting on the system along the inclined plane is zero.

The downward force along the incline due to gravity is $(m_1 + m_2)g \sin\theta$.

The upward force along the incline due to the compressed spring is $kx$, where $x$ is the compression of the spring.

Equating these forces:

$kx = (m_1 + m_2)g \sin\theta$

$x = \dfrac{(m_1 + m_2)g \sin\theta}{k}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $m_1$ is fastened to a spring on an incline of angle $\theta$, and a block of mass $m_2$ is placed against it. From the equilibrium position, the blocks are pushed a further distance of $(2/k)(m_1 + m_2) g \sin\theta$ against the spring and then released. Identify the position where the two blocks separate.
options: At a distance of $\dfrac{(m_1 + m_2) g \sin\theta}{k}$ above the natural length
At the point of maximum compression
When the spring acquires its natural length
questions.solution:
Let $x$ be the compression of the spring at any instant.

The equation of motion for the combined system of mass $(m_1 + m_2)$ is:

$kx - (m_1 + m_2)g \sin\theta = (m_1 + m_2)a$

where $a$ is the acceleration of the blocks up the incline.

The acceleration is:

$a = \dfrac{kx}{m_1 + m_2} - g \sin\theta$

For block $m_2$, the forces acting along the incline are the normal force $N$ exerted by $m_1$ and the component of gravity $m_2 g \sin\theta$.

The equation of motion for $m_2$ is:

$N - m_2 g \sin\theta = m_2 a$

Substituting the value of $a$:

$N = m_2 (a + g \sin\theta) = m_2 \left( \dfrac{kx}{m_1 + m_2} - g \sin\theta + g \sin\theta \right) = \dfrac{m_2 kx}{m_1 + m_2}$

The blocks separate when the normal force $N$ becomes zero.

$N = 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{m_2 kx}{m_1 + m_2} = 0 \Rightarrow x = 0$

This means the blocks separate when the spring acquires its natural length.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $m_1$ is fastened to a spring on an incline of angle $\theta$, and a block of mass $m_2$ is placed against it. The blocks are pushed from equilibrium by a further distance of $(2/k)(m_1 + m_2) g \sin\theta$ against the spring and released. What is the common speed of the blocks at the moment they separate?
questions.solution:
Let the compression of the spring be $x$. The equilibrium position of the system of two blocks is given by balancing the forces along the incline:

$k x_{eq} = (m_1 + m_2) g \sin\theta \Rightarrow x_{eq} = \dfrac{(m_1 + m_2) g \sin\theta}{k}$

The blocks are pushed a further distance $A$ from equilibrium, which becomes the amplitude of their simple harmonic motion:

$A = \dfrac{2(m_1 + m_2) g \sin\theta}{k}$

The blocks move together up the incline. Let $N$ be the normal force between the blocks. The equation of motion for block $m_2$ is:

$N - m_2 g \sin\theta = m_2 a$

The blocks separate when the normal force becomes zero ($N = 0$), which gives the acceleration at the moment of separation:

$a = -g \sin\theta$

For the combined system, the equation of motion is:

$k x - (m_1 + m_2) g \sin\theta = (m_1 + m_2) a$

Substituting $a = -g \sin\theta$, we get:

$k x - (m_1 + m_2) g \sin\theta = -(m_1 + m_2) g \sin\theta \Rightarrow k x = 0 \Rightarrow x = 0$

Thus, the blocks separate when the spring reaches its natural length. The natural length is at a distance $x_{eq}$ from the equilibrium position. The speed of the blocks at this position can be found using the velocity formula for simple harmonic motion, $v = \omega \sqrt{A^2 - y^2}$, where $y = x_{eq}$ is the displacement from equilibrium:

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m_1 + m_2}} \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{2(m_1 + m_2) g \sin\theta}{k}\right)^2 - \left(\dfrac{(m_1 + m_2) g \sin\theta}{k}\right)^2}$

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m_1 + m_2}} \sqrt{\dfrac{3(m_1 + m_2)^2 g^2 \sin^2\theta}{k^2}}$

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{3(m_1 + m_2)}{k}} g \sin\theta$

Answer: $\sqrt{\dfrac{3(m_1 + m_2)}{k}} g \sin\theta$

questions.q: As shown in the figure, a spring with constant $k = 100 \text{ N/m}$ is attached to a block of mass $M = 1 \text{ kg}$. A constant force $F = 10 \text{ N}$ acts on the block. While the block is in its equilibrium position, a sharp blow by an external agent imparts a speed of $2 \text{ m/s}$ to the block towards the left. Which of the following statements are correct?
options: The time period of the resulting simple harmonic motion is $\dfrac{\pi}{5} \text{ s}$.
The amplitude of the resulting simple harmonic motion is $20 \text{ cm}$.
The potential energy of the spring when the block is at the right extreme is $2.5 \text{ J}$.
The potential energy of the spring when the block is at the left extreme is $4.5 \text{ J}$.
questions.solution:
At the equilibrium position, the spring force balances the constant external force $F$. Let the compression in the spring be $x_0$.

$k x_0 = F \Rightarrow 100 x_0 = 10 \Rightarrow x_0 = 0.1 \text{ m} = 10 \text{ cm}$

The angular frequency of the SHM is $\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{M}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{100}{1}} = 10 \text{ rad/s}$.

The time period is $T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega} = \dfrac{2\pi}{10} = \dfrac{\pi}{5} \text{ s}$.

Since the blow is given at the equilibrium position, the imparted speed is the maximum velocity of the SHM.

$v_{max} = A\omega \Rightarrow 2 = A \times 10 \Rightarrow A = 0.2 \text{ m} = 20 \text{ cm}$

The block oscillates about the equilibrium position ($10 \text{ cm}$ compression) with an amplitude of $20 \text{ cm}$.

At the left extreme, the spring is further compressed. The maximum compression is $x_{left} = x_0 + A = 10 \text{ cm} + 20 \text{ cm} = 30 \text{ cm} = 0.3 \text{ m}$.

The potential energy of the spring at the left extreme is $U_{left} = \dfrac{1}{2} k x_{left}^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 100 \times (0.3)^2 = 4.5 \text{ J}$.

At the right extreme, the position of the block is $x_{right} = x_0 - A = 10 \text{ cm} - 20 \text{ cm} = -10 \text{ cm}$. This corresponds to an extension of $10 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$.

The potential energy of the spring at the right extreme is $U_{right} = \dfrac{1}{2} k x_{right}^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 100 \times (-0.1)^2 = 0.5 \text{ J}$.

Answer: The time period of the resulting simple harmonic motion is $\dfrac{\pi}{5} \text{ s}$.; The amplitude of the resulting simple harmonic motion is $20 \text{ cm}$.; The potential energy of the spring when the block is at the left extreme is $4.5 \text{ J}$.

This indicates that the springs are connected in parallel.

The time period of oscillation $T$ for a spring-mass system is given by:

For the middle arrangement (b), let the mass $m$ be displaced by a small distance $x$ to the right from its equilibrium position.

The left spring gets stretched by $x$, so it exerts a restoring force $F_1 = k_1 x$ towards the left.

The right spring gets compressed by $x$, so it exerts a restoring force $F_2 = k_2 x$ towards the left.

The net restoring force acting on the mass is $F = -(F_1 + F_2) = -(k_1 x + k_2 x) = -(k_1 + k_2)x$.

Comparing this with $F = -k_{eq} x$, we get the equivalent spring constant $k_{eq} = k_1 + k_2$.

The time period of oscillation is given by $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k_{eq}}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k_1 + k_2}}$.

questions.q: As shown in the figure, the spring is unstretched when a man begins pulling on the cord. The mass of the block is $M$. Provided the man exerts a constant force $F$, determine the amplitude and the time period of the block's motion.
questions.solution:
Let $x$ be the displacement of the block from its initial unstretched position.
The equation of motion for the block is given by:
$M \ddot{x} = F - kx$

This can be rewritten as:
$M \ddot{x} = -k\left(x - \dfrac{F}{k}\right)$

This equation represents Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) with a shifted equilibrium position. The new equilibrium position is where the net force is zero, i.e., $x_0 = \dfrac{F}{k}$.

Since the block starts from rest at the unstretched position ($x = 0$), this initial position is one of the extreme positions of the SHM. The amplitude $A$ of the motion is the distance between the extreme position and the equilibrium position:
$A = \left| x_0 - 0 \right| = \dfrac{F}{k}$

The time period of a spring-mass system depends only on the mass $M$ and the spring constant $k$, and is independent of any constant external force applied to it. Therefore, the time period is:
$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{M}{k}}$

questions.q: The spring is unstretched at the moment a man starts pulling on the cord. The block has a mass $M$. If the man applies a constant force $F$, calculate the energy stored in the spring when the block passes through its equilibrium position.
questions.solution:
Let the equilibrium position of the block be at a displacement $x$ from its initial unstretched position.

At the equilibrium position, the net force acting on the block is zero. The constant force $F$ applied by the man is balanced by the restoring force of the spring.

$F = kx$

$\Rightarrow x = \dfrac{F}{k}$

The energy stored in the spring at this position is the elastic potential energy, given by:

$U = \dfrac{1}{2}kx^2$

Substituting the value of $x$:

$U = \dfrac{1}{2}k\left(\dfrac{F}{k}\right)^2$

$U = \dfrac{1}{2}k\left(\dfrac{F^2}{k^2}\right)$

$U = \dfrac{F^2}{2k}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A man starts pulling on the cord when the spring is in its unstretched state. The block has a mass of $M$. Given that the man exerts a constant force $F$, determine the kinetic energy of the block at the instant it passes through the equilibrium position.
questions.solution:
The equilibrium position of the block is reached when the net force acting on it is zero. At this position, the constant applied force $F$ is balanced by the restoring force of the spring.

$F = kx_0 \Rightarrow x_0 = \dfrac{F}{k}$

According to the work-energy theorem, the net work done on the block equals its change in kinetic energy:

$W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$

The work done by the constant force $F$ is:

$W_F = F x_0 = F \left(\dfrac{F}{k}\right) = \dfrac{F^2}{k}$

The work done by the spring force is:

$W_s = -\dfrac{1}{2} k x_0^2 = -\dfrac{1}{2} k \left(\dfrac{F}{k}\right)^2 = -\dfrac{F^2}{2k}$

Since the block starts from rest, its initial kinetic energy is zero. The kinetic energy $K$ at the equilibrium position is:

$K = W_F + W_s = \dfrac{F^2}{k} - \dfrac{F^2}{2k} = \dfrac{F^2}{2k}$

questions.q: A particle of mass $m$ is connected to three springs $A$, $B$, and $C$ having equal force constants $k$, as shown in the figure. If the particle is pushed slightly against spring $C$ and then released, determine its time period of oscillation.
questions.solution:
Let the mass be at the origin $(0,0)$.

The directions of the springs are:
Spring A: along the positive x-axis ($\hat{i}$)
Spring B: along the positive y-axis ($\hat{j}$)
Spring C: at $45^\circ$ to the negative x-axis, along $-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{i} - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{j}$

When the particle is displaced by a small distance $x$ against spring C, the displacement vector is:
$\vec{s} = x\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{i} - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{j}\right)$

The extensions (or compressions) in the springs are the components of $\vec{s}$ along their respective directions:
For spring C, the displacement is directly along its axis, so it is compressed by $x$. The restoring force is $F_C = kx$ directed towards the origin.
For spring A, the extension is the magnitude of the component of $\vec{s}$ along $\hat{i}$, which is $x \cos 45^\circ = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{2}}$. The restoring force is $F_A = \dfrac{kx}{\sqrt{2}}$ along $\hat{i}$.
For spring B, the extension is the magnitude of the component of $\vec{s}$ along $\hat{j}$, which is $x \cos 45^\circ = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{2}}$. The restoring force is $F_B = \dfrac{kx}{\sqrt{2}}$ along $\hat{j}$.

The net restoring force along the line of displacement (towards the origin) is the sum of the components of these forces along that line:
$F_{net} = F_C + F_A \cos 45^\circ + F_B \cos 45^\circ$
$F_{net} = kx + \left(\dfrac{kx}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) + \left(\dfrac{kx}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$
$F_{net} = kx + \dfrac{kx}{2} + \dfrac{kx}{2} = 2kx$

The effective spring constant is $k_{eff} = 2k$.

The time period of oscillation is:
$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k_{eff}}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{2k}}$

Answer: $2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{2k}}$

questions.q: Three springs $A$, $B$, and $C$, each having a force constant $k$, are attached to a particle of mass $m$. Initially, the angle between any two springs is $120^\circ$. If the particle is slightly pushed against spring $C$ and then released, determine its time period of oscillation.
questions.solution:
Let the displacement of the particle be $x$ towards spring $C$.

The compression in spring $C$ is $x$. The restoring force exerted by spring $C$ is $F_C = kx$, directed opposite to the displacement.

The angle between the line of action of spring $C$ and those of springs $A$ and $B$ is $120^\circ$.

The extension in springs $A$ and $B$ is the component of displacement along their respective lengths, which is $x \cos(180^\circ - 120^\circ) = x \cos 60^\circ = \dfrac{x}{2}$.

The restoring force exerted by each of springs $A$ and $B$ is $F_A = F_B = k\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)$, directed towards their respective fixed ends.

The net restoring force from springs $A$ and $B$ along the direction opposite to the displacement is:

$F_{A,B} = F_A \cos 60^\circ + F_B \cos 60^\circ = 2 \left(\dfrac{kx}{2}\right) \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{kx}{2}$

The total restoring force on the particle is:

$F_{net} = F_C + F_{A,B} = kx + \dfrac{kx}{2} = \dfrac{3kx}{2}$

The effective spring constant of the system is $k_{eff} = \dfrac{3k}{2}$.

The time period of oscillation is given by:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k_{eff}}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{2m}{3k}}$

questions.q: Initially, all the springs displayed in the figure are unstretched when a man begins pulling the block. The man applies a constant force $F$ to the block. Determine the amplitude and the frequency of the block's motion.
options: Amplitude: $\dfrac{F(k_2 + k_3)}{k_1 k_2 + k_2 k_3 + k_3 k_1}$, Frequency: $\dfrac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\dfrac{M(k_2 + k_3)}{k_1 k_2 + k_2 k_3 + k_3 k_1}}$

Amplitude: $\dfrac{F(k_2 + k_3)}{k_1 k_2 + k_2 k_3 + k_3 k_1}$, Frequency: $\dfrac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\dfrac{k_1 k_2 + k_2 k_3 + k_3 k_1}{M(k_2 + k_3)}}$
Amplitude: $\dfrac{F}{k_1 + k_2 + k_3}$, Frequency: $\dfrac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\dfrac{k_1 + k_2 + k_3}{M}}$
questions.solution:
The springs $k_2$ and $k_3$ are connected in series. Their equivalent spring constant is:

$k_{23} = \dfrac{k_2 k_3}{k_2 + k_3}$

This combination is connected in parallel with spring $k_1$. The total equivalent spring constant of the system is:

$k_{eq} = k_1 + k_{23} = k_1 + \dfrac{k_2 k_3}{k_2 + k_3} = \dfrac{k_1 k_2 + k_2 k_3 + k_3 k_1}{k_2 + k_3}$

When a constant force $F$ is applied to the block, the equilibrium position shifts by a distance $x_0$ given by:

$x_0 = \dfrac{F}{k_{eq}}$

Since the block is initially at rest at the unstretched position, it will perform simple harmonic motion about the new equilibrium position. The amplitude $A$ of this motion is equal to the shift in the equilibrium position:

$A = x_0 = \dfrac{F}{k_{eq}} = \dfrac{F(k_2 + k_3)}{k_1 k_2 + k_2 k_3 + k_3 k_1}$

The frequency of the oscillation is given by:

$f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\dfrac{k_{eq}}{M}} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\dfrac{k_1 k_2 + k_2 k_3 + k_3 k_1}{M(k_2 + k_3)}}$

questions.q: Determine the time period of the mass $m$, assuming the string, spring, and pulley shown in the figure are light.
questions.solution:
Let the equilibrium extension of the spring be $x_0$.

At equilibrium, the tension in the string balances the weight of the mass $m$.

$T_0 = mg$

The tension is also equal to the spring force.

$T_0 = kx_0 \Rightarrow kx_0 = mg$

When the mass $m$ is displaced downwards by a distance $x$, the string pulls the spring upwards by the same distance $x$.

The new extension of the spring becomes $x_0 + x$.

The new tension in the string is $T = k(x_0 + x)$.

The net restoring force acting on the mass $m$ in the downward direction is:

$F = mg - T$

$F = mg - k(x_0 + x)$

Substituting $mg = kx_0$:

$F = kx_0 - kx_0 - kx = -kx$

The acceleration of the mass is $a = \dfrac{F}{m} = -\dfrac{k}{m}x$.

This is the equation of a simple harmonic motion $a = -\omega^2 x$, where $\omega^2 = \dfrac{k}{m}$.

The time period of oscillation is given by $T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}$.

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$

questions.q: The string and the spring depicted in the figure are light. Determine the time period of the mass $m$, assuming the pulley has a radius $r$ and a moment of inertia $I$ about its axis, and the string does not slip over it.
questions.solution:
Let the mass $m$ be displaced downwards by a small distance $x$ from its equilibrium position. The velocity of the mass is $v = \dot{x}$.

Since the string is inextensible and does not slip, the pulley rotates by an angle $\theta = x/r$, and its angular velocity is $\omega = v/r$. The spring is stretched by an additional amount $x$.

The total mechanical energy of the system is:

$E = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}k(x_0 + x)^2 - mgx$

where $x_0$ is the initial extension of the spring in equilibrium, satisfying $kx_0 = mg$.

Substituting $\omega = v/r$ and expanding the potential energy term:

$E = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(m + \dfrac{I}{r^2}\right) v^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}k x_0^2 + k x_0 x + \dfrac{1}{2}k x^2 - mgx$

Since $kx_0 = mg$, the terms $k x_0 x$ and $-mgx$ cancel out:

$E = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(m + \dfrac{I}{r^2}\right) v^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}k x^2 + \text{constant}$

Differentiating the total energy with respect to time ($\dfrac{dE}{dt} = 0$) gives:

$\left(m + \dfrac{I}{r^2}\right) v \dfrac{dv}{dt} + k x \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 0$

Using $v = \dfrac{dx}{dt}$ and $a = \dfrac{dv}{dt}$, we get:

$\left(m + \dfrac{I}{r^2}\right) a + k x = 0 \Rightarrow a = -\dfrac{k}{m + I/r^2} x$

Comparing this with the standard equation of SHM $a = -\omega^2 x$, the angular frequency is:

$\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m + I/r^2}}$

The time period of oscillation is:

$T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m + I/r^2}{k}}$

questions.solution:
When the rectangular plate is given a small displacement within its plane such that the strings remain taut, the two strings, the ceiling, and the top edge of the plate form a parallelogram.

Because the opposite sides of this linkage are equal (the strings both have length $L$, and the distance between them is $d$ at both the ceiling and the plate), the plate undergoes pure translational motion without any rotation. Its orientation remains horizontal throughout the motion.

Since the plate translates purely, every point on the plate, including its center of mass, moves in a circular arc of radius $L$.

Let the strings make a small angle $\theta$ with the vertical. The horizontal displacement of the center of mass is $x = L\sin\theta \approx L\theta$.

The restoring force acting on the plate is the horizontal component of the tension. Alternatively, considering the center of mass, the restoring force is:
$F = -Mg \sin\theta \approx -Mg\theta$

Substituting $\theta = \dfrac{x}{L}$, we get:
$F = -Mg \left(\dfrac{x}{L}\right)$

The acceleration of the plate is:
$a = \dfrac{F}{M} = -\left(\dfrac{g}{L}\right)x$

This represents simple harmonic motion with angular frequency $\omega^2 = \dfrac{g}{L}$.

Therefore, the time period of the motion is:
$T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}$

questions.q: Observe the setup shown in the figure. The blocks are given slight displacements in opposite directions and then released, causing them to execute simple harmonic motion. Calculate the time period of the resulting motion.
questions.solution:
For a two-body oscillator system, the time period of oscillation is given by $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{\mu}{k}}$, where $\mu$ is the reduced mass of the system.

The reduced mass $\mu$ for two masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ is $\mu = \dfrac{m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}$.

Given $m_1 = m$ and $m_2 = m$, we get:

$\mu = \dfrac{m \cdot m}{m + m} = \dfrac{m^2}{2m} = \dfrac{m}{2}$

Substituting the value of $\mu$ into the time period formula:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m/2}{k}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{2k}}$

questions.q: A $1 \text{ kg}$ block executes simple harmonic motion with an amplitude of $0.1 \text{ m}$ on a smooth horizontal surface, driven by the restoring force of a spring having a spring constant of $100 \text{ N/m}$. At the instant the block passes through its mean position, a $3 \text{ kg}$ block is gently placed on top of it. Assuming the two blocks subsequently move together as a single unit, determine the new frequency and the amplitude of the motion.
questions.solution:
Initial mass $m_1 = 1 \text{ kg}$, amplitude $A_1 = 0.1 \text{ m}$, and spring constant $k = 100 \text{ N/m}$.

The angular frequency of the initial block is:
$\omega_1 = \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m_1}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{100}{1}} = 10 \text{ rad/s}$

The velocity of the block at the mean position is:
$v_1 = A_1 \omega_1 = 0.1 \times 10 = 1 \text{ m/s}$

When the $3 \text{ kg}$ block is gently placed on the $1 \text{ kg}$ block at the mean position, the horizontal momentum of the system is conserved. Let $v_2$ be the new velocity at the mean position:
$m_1 v_1 = (m_1 + m_2) v_2$
$1 \times 1 = (1 + 3) v_2 \Rightarrow v_2 = 0.25 \text{ m/s}$

The new angular frequency of the system is:
$\omega_2 = \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m_1 + m_2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{100}{4}} = 5 \text{ rad/s}$

The new frequency is:
$f_2 = \dfrac{\omega_2}{2\pi} = \dfrac{5}{2\pi} \text{ Hz}$

The new amplitude $A_2$ can be found using the relation $v_2 = A_2 \omega_2$ at the mean position:
$0.25 = A_2 \times 5 \Rightarrow A_2 = 0.05 \text{ m} = 5 \text{ cm}$

questions.q: As shown in the figure, the left block travels at a speed $v$ towards the right block, which is placed in equilibrium. All collisions that occur are elastic and the surfaces are frictionless. Determine the time period of the periodic motions of the two blocks. Neglect the widths of the blocks.
questions.solution:
Let the cycle begin when the left block moves from the left wall towards the right block with velocity $v$.

The distance to the right block is $L$. The time taken by the left block to reach the right block is:
$t_1 = \dfrac{L}{v}$

Since the collision is perfectly elastic and both blocks have the same mass $m$, they exchange their velocities upon impact. The left block comes to rest, and the right block acquires the velocity $v$ towards the right.

The right block then compresses the spring, comes to a momentary halt, and returns to its equilibrium position. This motion constitutes exactly half of a simple harmonic oscillation. The time taken for this half-cycle is:
$t_2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}} \right) = \pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$

When the right block returns to its equilibrium position, it has a velocity $v$ directed towards the left. It then collides elastically with the stationary left block. Velocities are exchanged once again: the right block comes to rest, and the left block acquires a velocity $v$ towards the left.

The left block travels the distance $L$ back to the left wall. The time taken for this return journey is:
$t_3 = \dfrac{L}{v}$

Upon reaching the left wall, the left block collides elastically with it and rebounds with velocity $v$ towards the right. This brings the system back to its exact initial state, completing one full cycle.

The total time period $T$ of the periodic motion is the sum of these time intervals:
$T = t_1 + t_2 + t_3$

$T = \dfrac{L}{v} + \pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}} + \dfrac{L}{v}$

$T = \pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}} + \dfrac{2L}{v}$

questions.q: Determine the time period of the particle's motion as depicted in the figure. Disregard the minor effect of the bend near the bottom.
questions.solution:
The time taken by the particle to slide down an incline of angle $\theta$ from a height $h$ is given by $t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2s}{a}}$, where $s = \dfrac{h}{\sin \theta}$ and $a = g \sin \theta$.

Thus, $t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g \sin^2 \theta}} = \dfrac{1}{\sin \theta} \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$.

The total time period $T$ of the motion consists of sliding down the first incline, sliding up the second incline, sliding down the second incline, and sliding up the first incline.

Therefore, $T = 2(t_1 + t_2) = 2 \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}} \left( \dfrac{1}{\sin \theta_1} + \dfrac{1}{\sin \theta_2} \right)$.

Given $h = 10 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$, $\theta_1 = 45^\circ$, $\theta_2 = 60^\circ$, and taking $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$T = 2 \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 0.1}{9.8}} \left( \dfrac{1}{\sin 45^\circ} + \dfrac{1}{\sin 60^\circ} \right)$

$T = 2 \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{49}} \left( \sqrt{2} + \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \right)$

$T = \dfrac{2}{7} \left( 1.414 + 1.155 \right)$

$T = \dfrac{2}{7} (2.569) \approx 0.734 \text{ s}$.

The closest value is $0.73 \text{ s}$.

questions.q: Assume all surfaces depicted in the diagram lack friction. The car has a mass $M$, the block has a mass $m$, and the spring possesses a force constant $k$. The system is released from rest with the spring initially stretched by a distance $x_0$. Determine the time period of the resulting simple harmonic motions.
questions.solution:
Let $x_1$ and $x_2$ be the displacements of the block of mass $m$ and the car of mass $M$ from their respective equilibrium positions.

Since no external horizontal force acts on the system, the center of mass remains stationary. Therefore:

$m x_1 + M x_2 = 0 \Rightarrow x_2 = -\dfrac{m}{M} x_1$

The net extension or compression in the spring is the relative displacement $x = x_1 - x_2$.

Substituting the value of $x_2$, we get:

$x = x_1 - \left(-\dfrac{m}{M} x_1\right) = x_1 \left(1 + \dfrac{m}{M}\right) = x_1 \left(\dfrac{M + m}{M}\right)$

The restoring force acting on the block of mass $m$ is $F = -kx$.

$F = -k \left(\dfrac{M + m}{M}\right) x_1$

The acceleration of the block is $a_1 = \dfrac{F}{m} = -\dfrac{k(M + m)}{mM} x_1$.

Comparing this with the standard equation of simple harmonic motion $a = -\omega^2 x$, we find the angular frequency $\omega$:

$\omega^2 = \dfrac{k(M + m)}{mM} \Rightarrow \omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{k(M + m)}{mM}}$

The time period of oscillation is given by $T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}$:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{mM}{k(M + m)}}$

Alternatively, this is a standard two-body oscillator problem where the time period is given by $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{\mu}{k}}$, with the reduced mass $\mu = \dfrac{mM}{M + m}$.

questions.q: A uniform plate of mass $M$ rests horizontally and symmetrically on two wheels that rotate in opposite directions, as shown in the figure. The distance between the wheels is $L$, and the coefficient of friction between the plate and each wheel is $\mu$. Determine the time period of oscillation of the plate if it is given a slight displacement along its length and then released.
questions.solution:
Let the center of mass (CM) of the plate be displaced by a distance $x$ towards the right from its equilibrium position.

The distance of the CM from the left wheel becomes $\dfrac{L}{2} + x$ and from the right wheel becomes $\dfrac{L}{2} - x$.

Let $N_1$ and $N_2$ be the normal reactions from the left and right wheels, respectively. For vertical equilibrium:

$N_1 + N_2 = Mg$

For rotational equilibrium about the CM, the net torque is zero:

$N_1 \left( \dfrac{L}{2} + x \right) = N_2 \left( \dfrac{L}{2} - x \right)$

Solving these two equations, we get:

$N_1 = \dfrac{Mg}{L} \left( \dfrac{L}{2} - x \right)$ and $N_2 = \dfrac{Mg}{L} \left( \dfrac{L}{2} + x \right)$

The wheels are rotating inwards, so the kinetic friction forces act towards the center. The left wheel exerts a force $f_1 = \mu N_1$ towards the right, and the right wheel exerts a force $f_2 = \mu N_2$ towards the left.

The net restoring force on the plate is:

$F = f_1 - f_2 = \mu N_1 - \mu N_2 = \mu (N_1 - N_2)$

Substituting the values of $N_1$ and $N_2$:

$F = \mu \dfrac{Mg}{L} \left[ \left( \dfrac{L}{2} - x \right) - \left( \dfrac{L}{2} + x \right) \right] = -\dfrac{2 \mu Mg}{L} x$

The acceleration of the plate is:

$a = \dfrac{F}{M} = -\left( \dfrac{2 \mu g}{L} \right) x$

This represents simple harmonic motion with $\omega^2 = \dfrac{2 \mu g}{L}$.

The time period of oscillation is:

$T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{L}{2 \mu g}}$

questions.q: A seconds pendulum is a pendulum having a time period equal to two seconds. These are the type utilized in pendulum clocks. Calculate the length of a seconds pendulum at a location where $g = \pi^2 \text{ m/s}^2$.
questions.solution:
The time period of a simple pendulum is given by $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}$.

For a seconds pendulum, the time period is $T = 2 \text{ s}$.

Substituting $T = 2 \text{ s}$ and $g = \pi^2 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$2 = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{L}{\pi^2}}$

$1 = \pi \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{L}}{\pi}\right)$

$1 = \sqrt{L}$

$L = 1 \text{ m}$

questions.q: The angle that the string of a simple pendulum makes with the vertical varies with time according to the equation $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{90} \sin[(\pi \text{ s}^{-1}) t]$. Determine the length of the pendulum, taking $g = \pi^2 \text{ m/s}^2$.
questions.solution:
The given equation for the angular displacement of the simple pendulum is $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{90} \sin(\pi t)$.

Comparing this with the standard equation of simple harmonic motion $\theta = \theta_0 \sin(\omega t)$, the angular frequency is $\omega = \pi \text{ rad/s}$.

The angular frequency of a simple pendulum is given by $\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{g}{l}}$.

Squaring both sides gives $\omega^2 = \dfrac{g}{l}$.

Rearranging for the length $l$, we get $l = \dfrac{g}{\omega^2}$.

Substituting $g = \pi^2 \text{ m/s}^2$ and $\omega = \pi \text{ rad/s}$ into the expression:

$l = \dfrac{\pi^2}{\pi^2} = 1 \text{ m}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A certain clock's pendulum has a time period of $2.04\text{ s}$. How fast or slow will the clock run over a $24$-hour period?
questions.solution:
A standard seconds pendulum has a time period $T = 2\text{ s}$.

The given pendulum has a time period $T' = 2.04\text{ s}$. Since $T' > T$, the pendulum takes more time to complete one oscillation, meaning the clock will run slow.

In a true time of $24\text{ hours}$ ($24 \times 3600 = 86400\text{ s}$), the number of oscillations made by the pendulum is:

$n = \dfrac{86400}{2.04}$

Since the clock registers $2\text{ s}$ for every oscillation, the time shown by the clock in $24\text{ hours}$ is:

$t_{\text{clock}} = n \times 2 = \dfrac{86400}{2.04} \times 2 = \dfrac{172800}{2.04}\text{ s}$

The time lost by the clock in $24\text{ hours}$ is the difference between the true time and the clock time:

$\Delta t = 86400 - \dfrac{172800}{2.04}$

$\Delta t = 86400 \left(1 - \dfrac{2}{2.04}\right) = 86400 \left(\dfrac{0.04}{2.04}\right)$

$\Delta t = \dfrac{3456}{2.04} \approx 1694.12\text{ s}$

Converting the time lost into minutes:

$\Delta t = \dfrac{1694.12}{60} \approx 28.235\text{ minutes}$

Therefore, the clock will run approximately $28.2\text{ minutes}$ slow.

Answer: $28.2\text{ minutes}$ slow

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A pendulum clock that gives correct time at a location where $g = 9.800 \text{ m/s}^2$ is transported to a new location, where it is observed to lose $24$ seconds over a period of $24$ hours. Determine the value of $g$ at this new location.
questions.solution:
The time period of a simple pendulum is given by $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}$.

Taking the natural logarithm and differentiating, we get the fractional change in the time period:

$\dfrac{\Delta T}{T} = -\dfrac{1}{2} \dfrac{\Delta g}{g}$

The time lost by the clock in a total time $t$ is given by $\Delta t = t \dfrac{\Delta T}{T}$.

Given that the clock loses $24$ seconds in $24$ hours ($86400$ seconds), the fractional change in the time period is:

$\dfrac{\Delta T}{T} = \dfrac{24}{86400} = \dfrac{1}{3600}$

Substituting this into the fractional change equation:

$\dfrac{1}{3600} = -\dfrac{1}{2} \dfrac{\Delta g}{g}$

$\Delta g = -g \times \dfrac{2}{3600} = -9.800 \times \dfrac{1}{1800} \approx -0.00544 \text{ m/s}^2$

The acceleration due to gravity at the new location is:

$g' = g + \Delta g = 9.800 - 0.00544 = 9.79456 \text{ m/s}^2$

Rounding to three decimal places, we get $g' \approx 9.795 \text{ m/s}^2$.

questions.solution:

Substituting the given values $L = 5.0 \text{ m}$ and $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\dfrac{9.8}{5.0}}$

$f = \dfrac{0.70}{\pi} \text{ Hz}$

The frequency of a simple pendulum is given by the formula:

$f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\dfrac{g'}{L}}$

Given the length of the pendulum $L = 5.0 \text{ m}$ and the acceleration due to gravity on the moon $g' = 1.67 \text{ m/s}^2$.

Approximating $1.67 \text{ m/s}^2$ as $\dfrac{5}{3} \text{ m/s}^2$ and substituting the values:

$f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\dfrac{5/3}{5}}$

$f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{3}}$

$f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi \sqrt{3}} \text{ Hz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In the string of an oscillating pendulum, the maximum tension is double the minimum tension. Determine the angular amplitude.
questions.solution:
Let the angular amplitude be $\theta_0$.

The tension in the string at an angle $\theta$ with the vertical is given by $T = mg \cos \theta + \dfrac{mv^2}{l}$.

By conservation of energy, the velocity $v$ at angle $\theta$ is given by $\dfrac{1}{2} m v^2 = mg l (\cos \theta - \cos \theta_0)$, which gives $v^2 = 2gl (\cos \theta - \cos \theta_0)$.

Substituting $v^2$ into the tension equation, we get $T = mg \cos \theta + 2mg (\cos \theta - \cos \theta_0) = mg (3 \cos \theta - 2 \cos \theta_0)$.

The maximum tension occurs at the lowest point ($\theta = 0$):
$T_{\max} = mg (3 - 2 \cos \theta_0)$

The minimum tension occurs at the extreme position ($\theta = \theta_0$):
$T_{\min} = mg (3 \cos \theta_0 - 2 \cos \theta_0) = mg \cos \theta_0$

Given that $T_{\max} = 2 T_{\min}$:
$mg (3 - 2 \cos \theta_0) = 2 mg \cos \theta_0$

$3 - 2 \cos \theta_0 = 2 \cos \theta_0$

$4 \cos \theta_0 = 3$

$\cos \theta_0 = \dfrac{3}{4}$

$\theta_0 = \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)$

questions.q: As illustrated in the figure, a small block undergoes back-and-forth oscillations on a smooth concave surface of radius $R$. Determine the time period for small oscillations.
questions.solution:
Let the block be displaced by a small angle $\theta$ from the lowest point (mean position).

The restoring force acting on the block along the tangential direction is:
$F = -mg \sin\theta$

For small oscillations, $\sin\theta \approx \theta$. Thus, the restoring force becomes:
$F = -mg \theta$

The displacement along the arc is $x = R\theta$, which implies $\theta = \dfrac{x}{R}$. Substituting this into the force equation gives:
$F = -mg \left(\dfrac{x}{R}\right)$

The acceleration of the block is:
$a = \dfrac{F}{m} = -\left(\dfrac{g}{R}\right) x$

Comparing this with the standard equation of simple harmonic motion $a = -\omega^2 x$, we get:
$\omega^2 = \dfrac{g}{R} \Rightarrow \omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{g}{R}}$

The time period of oscillation is:
$T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{R}{g}}$
