questions.q: A spherical ball of mass $m$ and radius $r$ rolls without slipping on a rough concave surface possessing a large radius $R$. It executes small oscillations about the lowest point. Determine the time period.
questions.solution:
Let $\theta$ be the angular displacement of the center of the ball from the vertical. The center of the ball moves in a circle of radius $R - r$.

The velocity of the center of the ball is $v = (R - r)\dot{\theta}$.

For pure rolling without slipping, the angular velocity of the ball about its center is $\omega = \dfrac{v}{r} = \dfrac{(R - r)\dot{\theta}}{r}$.

The total kinetic energy of the ball is:

$K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$

Substituting $I = \dfrac{2}{5}mr^2$ for a solid sphere:

$K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2}{5}mr^2\right)\left(\dfrac{v}{r}\right)^2 = \dfrac{7}{10}mv^2 = \dfrac{7}{10}m(R - r)^2\dot{\theta}^2$

The potential energy of the ball relative to its lowest position is:

$U = mg(R - r)(1 - \cos\theta)$

For small angles, $1 - \cos\theta \approx \dfrac{\theta^2}{2}$, so:

$U \approx \dfrac{1}{2}mg(R - r)\theta^2$

By conservation of mechanical energy, $E = K + U = \text{constant}$:

$\dfrac{7}{10}m(R - r)^2\dot{\theta}^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}mg(R - r)\theta^2 = \text{constant}$

Differentiating with respect to time $t$:

$\dfrac{7}{5}m(R - r)^2\dot{\theta}\ddot{\theta} + mg(R - r)\theta\dot{\theta} = 0$

$\ddot{\theta} + \dfrac{5g}{7(R - r)}\theta = 0$

Comparing with the standard equation of SHM $\ddot{\theta} + \omega_0^2\theta = 0$, we get the angular frequency:

$\omega_0 = \sqrt{\dfrac{5g}{7(R - r)}}$

The time period of oscillation is:

$T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega_0} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{7(R - r)}{5g}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A simple pendulum measuring $40 \text{ cm}$ in length is placed inside a deep mine. Assuming the mine's depth to be $1600 \text{ km}$, determine the time period of the pendulum at that location. The radius of the earth is $6400 \text{ km}$.
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity at a depth $d$ is given by:

$g' = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right)$

Substituting $d = 1600 \text{ km}$ and $R = 6400 \text{ km}$:

$g' = g\left(1 - \dfrac{1600}{6400}\right) = g\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{4}\right) = \dfrac{3g}{4}$

The time period of a simple pendulum is:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g'}}$

Given $L = 40 \text{ cm} = 0.4 \text{ m}$ and taking $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{0.4}{\dfrac{3 \times 9.8}{4}}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{1.6}{29.4}}$

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{0.0544} \approx 2 \times 3.14 \times 0.233 \approx 1.466 \text{ s}$

Rounding off to two decimal places, $T \approx 1.47 \text{ s}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Suppose a tunnel is excavated across the earth (radius $= R$) passing through its centre. Calculate the time a particle takes to traverse the length of the tunnel if it is projected into the tunnel with a speed of $\sqrt{gR}$.
questions.solution:
The gravitational force on a particle of mass $m$ at a distance $x$ from the centre of the earth is given by $F = -\dfrac{GMm}{R^3} x$.

The acceleration of the particle is $a = -\dfrac{GM}{R^3} x = -\dfrac{g}{R} x$.

This shows that the particle executes simple harmonic motion (SHM) with angular frequency $\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{g}{R}}$.

The velocity $v$ of a particle in SHM is related to its position $x$ and amplitude $A$ by the equation $v^2 = \omega^2 (A^2 - x^2)$.

Given that at the surface $x = R$, the velocity is $v = \sqrt{gR}$, we can find the amplitude $A$:

$gR = \dfrac{g}{R} (A^2 - R^2)$

$R^2 = A^2 - R^2 \Rightarrow A = \sqrt{2}R$

The position of the particle at any time $t$ can be written as $x = A \cos(\omega t + \phi)$.

At $t = 0$, the particle is at $x = R$ and moving towards the centre, so:

$R = \sqrt{2}R \cos\phi \Rightarrow \cos\phi = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Rightarrow \phi = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$

The particle reaches the other end of the tunnel when $x = -R$:

$-R = \sqrt{2}R \cos\left(\omega t + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$

$\cos\left(\omega t + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

The smallest positive phase corresponding to this position is $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$.

$\omega t + \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$

$\omega t = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

$t = \dfrac{\pi}{2\omega} = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \sqrt{\dfrac{R}{g}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Suppose a tunnel is excavated across the earth (radius $= R$) passing through its centre. Calculate the time a particle takes to traverse the length of the tunnel if it is released from a height $R$ above the tunnel.
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the Earth be $M$ and its radius be $R$. The particle is released from a height $R$ above the surface, so its initial distance from the center of the Earth is $2R$.

Using the principle of conservation of mechanical energy from the point of release to the surface of the Earth:

$E_i = E_f$

$-\dfrac{GMm}{2R} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R} + \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{GMm}{2R}$

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{R}} = \sqrt{gR}$

This is the velocity of the particle as it enters the tunnel. Inside the Earth, the gravitational force at a distance $x$ from the center is $F = -\dfrac{GMm}{R^3}x$.

The acceleration is $a = -\dfrac{g}{R}x$, which shows that the particle executes Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) with angular frequency $\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{g}{R}}$.

Using the velocity-position relation for SHM, $v^2 = \omega^2(A^2 - x^2)$, we can find the amplitude $A$ of the motion. At the surface ($x = R$), the velocity is $v = \sqrt{gR}$:

$gR = \dfrac{g}{R}(A^2 - R^2)$

$R^2 = A^2 - R^2 \Rightarrow A = R\sqrt{2}$

The time taken to traverse the tunnel is the time to travel from $x = R$ to $x = -R$. Using the equation of SHM $x = A\cos(\omega t + \phi)$:

At the entrance ($t = 0$), $x = R$ and the particle is moving towards the center:

$R = R\sqrt{2}\cos\phi \Rightarrow \cos\phi = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Rightarrow \phi = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$

At the exit, $x = -R$:

$-R = R\sqrt{2}\cos\left(\omega t + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \Rightarrow \cos\left(\omega t + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

The next phase where the cosine is $-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ is $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$:

$\omega t + \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{3\pi}{4} \Rightarrow \omega t = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

$t = \dfrac{\pi}{2\omega} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{\dfrac{R}{g}}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \sqrt{\dfrac{R}{g}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Suppose a tunnel is excavated across the earth (radius $= R$) passing through its centre. Calculate the time a particle takes to traverse the length of the tunnel if it is thrown vertically upward along the length of the tunnel with a speed of $\sqrt{gR}$.
questions.solution:
The acceleration of a particle at a distance $x$ from the centre of the earth inside a tunnel is given by $a = -\dfrac{g}{R}x$.

This represents simple harmonic motion (SHM) with an angular frequency $\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{g}{R}}$.

The general equation for the position of a particle in SHM is:

$x(t) = x_0 \cos(\omega t) + \dfrac{v_0}{\omega} \sin(\omega t)$

Let the particle be thrown from one end of the tunnel, so its initial position is $x_0 = -R$. It is thrown along the length of the tunnel with an initial speed $v_0 = \sqrt{gR}$.

Substituting these initial conditions into the equation of motion:

$x(t) = -R \cos(\omega t) + \dfrac{\sqrt{gR}}{\sqrt{g/R}} \sin(\omega t)$

$x(t) = -R \cos(\omega t) + R \sin(\omega t)$

To traverse the entire length of the tunnel, the particle must reach the other end, which corresponds to $x(t) = R$. Substituting this into the equation:

$R = -R \cos(\omega t) + R \sin(\omega t)$

$\sin(\omega t) - \cos(\omega t) = 1$

Multiplying and dividing by $\sqrt{2}$:

$\sqrt{2} \left( \sin(\omega t) \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - \cos(\omega t) \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right) = 1$

$\sqrt{2} \sin\left(\omega t - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 1$

$\sin\left(\omega t - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

The smallest positive angle satisfying this is:

$\omega t - \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$

$\omega t = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

Substituting $\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{g}{R}}$:

$t = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \sqrt{\dfrac{R}{g}}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \sqrt{\dfrac{R}{g}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Suppose a tunnel is excavated along a chord of the earth at a perpendicular distance $R/2$ from the earth's centre, where $R$ is the radius of the earth. The wall of the tunnel is frictionless. Determine the magnitude of the gravitational force exerted by the earth on a particle of mass $m$ placed in the tunnel at a distance $x$ from the centre of the tunnel.
questions.solution:
Let $O$ be the centre of the earth and $C$ be the centre of the tunnel.

The perpendicular distance from the centre of the earth to the tunnel is $OC = \dfrac{R}{2}$.

Let $P$ be the position of the particle in the tunnel. The distance of the particle from the centre of the tunnel is $CP = x$.

In the right-angled triangle $OCP$, the distance $r$ of the particle from the centre of the earth is given by:

$r = OP = \sqrt{OC^2 + CP^2} = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{R}{2}\right)^2 + x^2} = \sqrt{x^2 + \dfrac{R^2}{4}}$

The magnitude of the gravitational force exerted by the earth on a particle of mass $m$ at a distance $r$ ($r < R$) from its centre is:

$F = \dfrac{GMm}{R^3} r$

Substituting the value of $r$, we get:

$F = \dfrac{GMm}{R^3} \sqrt{x^2 + \dfrac{R^2}{4}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Suppose a tunnel is excavated along a chord of the earth at a perpendicular distance $R/2$ from the earth's centre, where $R$ is the radius of the earth. The wall of the tunnel is frictionless. A particle of mass $m$ is placed in the tunnel at a distance $x$ from the centre of the tunnel. Find the magnitudes of the components of the earth's gravitational force on the particle along the tunnel and perpendicular to the tunnel, respectively.
questions.solution:
Let the centre of the earth be the origin $(0,0)$. Let the tunnel be parallel to the x-axis at a perpendicular distance $y = \dfrac{R}{2}$.

The position vector of the particle at a distance $x$ from the centre of the tunnel is given by $\vec{r} = x \hat{i} + \dfrac{R}{2} \hat{j}$.

The gravitational force on a particle of mass $m$ inside the earth at a position vector $\vec{r}$ from the centre is directed towards the centre and is given by:

$\vec{F} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R^3} \vec{r}$

Substituting the position vector $\vec{r}$ into the force equation, we get:

$\vec{F} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R^3} \left( x \hat{i} + \dfrac{R}{2} \hat{j} \right)$

$\vec{F} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R^3} x \hat{i} - \dfrac{GMm}{2R^2} \hat{j}$

The magnitude of the component of the force along the tunnel (x-direction) is:

$F_{\parallel} = \dfrac{GMm}{R^3} x$

The magnitude of the component of the force perpendicular to the tunnel (y-direction) is:

$F_{\perp} = \dfrac{GMm}{2R^2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Suppose a tunnel is excavated along a chord of the earth at a perpendicular distance $R/2$ from the earth's centre, where $R$ is the radius of the earth. The wall of the tunnel is frictionless. Determine the normal force exerted by the wall on a particle of mass $m$ placed in the tunnel at a distance $x$ from the centre of the tunnel.
questions.solution:
Let the centre of the earth be the origin $(0,0)$. The tunnel is excavated along a chord at a perpendicular distance $\dfrac{R}{2}$ from the centre, so we can assume the tunnel lies along the line $y = \dfrac{R}{2}$.

The position vector of the particle at a distance $x$ from the centre of the tunnel is given by $\vec{r} = x \hat{i} + \dfrac{R}{2} \hat{j}$.

The gravitational force on a particle of mass $m$ inside the earth at a position $\vec{r}$ is directed towards the centre of the earth and is given by:

$\vec{F}_g = -\dfrac{GMm}{R^3} \vec{r}$

Substituting the position vector of the particle:

$\vec{F}_g = -\dfrac{GMm}{R^3} \left( x \hat{i} + \dfrac{R}{2} \hat{j} \right)$

The force has two components:
1. Along the tunnel (x-direction): $F_{\parallel} = -\dfrac{GMmx}{R^3} \hat{i}$, which provides the restoring force for oscillatory motion.
2. Perpendicular to the tunnel (y-direction): $F_{\perp} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R^3} \left( \dfrac{R}{2} \right) \hat{j} = -\dfrac{GMm}{2R^2} \hat{j}$.

Since the particle is constrained to move only along the tunnel, the normal force $N$ exerted by the frictionless wall must balance the perpendicular component of the gravitational force.

Therefore, the magnitude of the normal force is:

$N = |F_{\perp}| = \dfrac{GMm}{2R^2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Suppose a tunnel is excavated along a chord of the earth at a perpendicular distance $R/2$ from the earth's centre, where $R$ is the radius of the earth. The wall of the tunnel is frictionless. Determine the magnitude of the resultant force acting on a particle of mass $m$ placed in the tunnel at a distance $x$ from the centre of the tunnel.
questions.solution:
Let the centre of the earth be the origin $O$. The tunnel is excavated along a chord at a perpendicular distance $\dfrac{R}{2}$ from $O$.

Let the centre of the tunnel be $C$. The distance $OC = \dfrac{R}{2}$.

When the particle is at a distance $x$ from $C$, its distance $r$ from the centre of the earth is given by:

$r = \sqrt{x^2 + \left(\dfrac{R}{2}\right)^2}$

The gravitational force exerted by the earth on the particle is directed towards the centre of the earth and its magnitude is:

$F_g = \dfrac{GMmr}{R^3}$

This force can be resolved into two components:
1. Along the tunnel (towards $C$): $F_{\parallel} = F_g \times \dfrac{x}{r} = \left(\dfrac{GMmr}{R^3}\right) \left(\dfrac{x}{r}\right) = \dfrac{GMm}{R^3}x$
2. Perpendicular to the tunnel: $F_{\perp} = F_g \times \dfrac{R/2}{r} = \dfrac{GMm}{R^3}\left(\dfrac{R}{2}\right)$

Since the wall of the tunnel is frictionless, it provides a normal reaction $N$ which exactly balances the perpendicular component of the gravitational force ($N = F_{\perp}$).

Therefore, the resultant force acting on the particle is solely the component of the gravitational force along the tunnel.

Magnitude of the resultant force $= \dfrac{GMm}{R^3}x$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Suppose a tunnel is excavated along a chord of the earth at a perpendicular distance $R/2$ from the earth's centre, where $R$ is the radius of the earth. The wall of the tunnel is frictionless. A particle of mass $m$ is placed in the tunnel at a distance $x$ from the centre of the tunnel and released. The particle exhibits simple harmonic motion. Find the time period of this motion.
questions.solution:
Let the centre of the earth be $O$ and the centre of the tunnel be $C$. The distance $OC = R/2$.

When the particle is at a distance $x$ from $C$, its distance from the centre of the earth is $r = \sqrt{x^2 + (R/2)^2}$.

The gravitational force acting on the particle of mass $m$ at a distance $r$ from the centre of the earth is directed towards $O$ and is given by:

$F = \dfrac{GMmr}{R^3}$

The component of this force along the tunnel acts as the restoring force. From the geometry of the right-angled triangle formed by $O, C$, and the particle, the component of the force along the tunnel is:

$F_x = -F \cos \theta = -F \left(\dfrac{x}{r}\right)$

Substituting the value of $F$, we get:

$F_x = -\left(\dfrac{GMmr}{R^3}\right) \left(\dfrac{x}{r}\right) = -\dfrac{GMm}{R^3} x$

Since the restoring force is proportional to the displacement $x$, the particle executes simple harmonic motion with an effective force constant $k = \dfrac{GMm}{R^3}$.

The time period of the simple harmonic motion is:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{R^3}{GM}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A simple pendulum of length $l$ is attached to the ceiling of an elevator. Determine the time period of small oscillations if the elevator is going up with an acceleration $a_0$.
questions.solution:
In the frame of reference of the elevator accelerating upwards with an acceleration $a_0$, a pseudo force $ma_0$ acts downwards on the pendulum bob of mass $m$.

The true gravitational force $mg$ also acts downwards.

The effective weight of the bob is $W_{\text{eff}} = mg + ma_0 = m(g + a_0)$.

The effective acceleration due to gravity is $g_{\text{eff}} = g + a_0$.

The time period of a simple pendulum is given by $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g_{\text{eff}}}}$.

Substituting the value of $g_{\text{eff}}$, we get $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g + a_0}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A simple pendulum of length $l$ hangs from the ceiling of an elevator. Calculate the time period of small oscillations assuming the elevator is going down with an acceleration $a_0$.
questions.solution:
In the frame of reference of the elevator, a pseudo force $m a_0$ acts on the pendulum bob in the upward direction, opposite to the downward acceleration of the elevator.

The true gravitational force $mg$ acts in the downward direction.

The net effective force on the bob is $F_{eff} = mg - m a_0 = m(g - a_0)$.

The effective acceleration due to gravity is $g_{eff} = g - a_0$.

The time period of a simple pendulum is given by $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g_{eff}}}$.

Substituting the value of $g_{eff}$, we get $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g - a_0}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A simple pendulum of length $l$ is suspended from the ceiling of an elevator. Find the time period of small oscillations given that the elevator travels with a uniform velocity.
questions.solution:
Since the elevator is moving with a uniform velocity, its acceleration is zero.

The effective acceleration due to gravity inside the elevator is $g_{eff} = g$.

The time period of a simple pendulum is given by $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g_{eff}}}$.

Substituting $g_{eff} = g$, we get $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Suspended from an elevator's ceiling, a simple pendulum of length $1$ feet requires $\pi/3$ seconds to complete one oscillation. Determine the acceleration of the elevator.
questions.solution:
The time period of a simple pendulum in an accelerating elevator is given by $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g_{\text{eff}}}}$.

Given $T = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ s and $l = 1$ ft, substituting these values:

$\dfrac{\pi}{3} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{g_{\text{eff}}}}$

Squaring both sides:

$\dfrac{1}{9} = \dfrac{4}{g_{\text{eff}}}$

$g_{\text{eff}} = 36 \text{ ft/s}^2$

The standard acceleration due to gravity is $g = 32 \text{ ft/s}^2$. Since $g_{\text{eff}} > g$, the elevator must be accelerating upwards.

For an elevator accelerating upwards with acceleration $a$, $g_{\text{eff}} = g + a$.

$36 = 32 + a$

$a = 4 \text{ ft/s}^2$

The acceleration of the elevator is $4 \text{ ft/s}^2$ upwards.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A simple pendulum fixed inside a car has a time period of $4$ seconds while the car is travelling uniformly on a horizontal road. Upon pressing the accelerator, the time period shifts to $3.99$ seconds. Determine the acceleration of the car using an approximate analysis.
questions.solution:
The initial time period of the simple pendulum is given by:

$T_1 = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}} = 4$

When the car accelerates with acceleration $a$, the effective acceleration due to gravity becomes:

$g_{eff} = \sqrt{g^2 + a^2} = g \left(1 + \dfrac{a^2}{g^2}\right)^{1/2}$

The new time period is given by:

$T_2 = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g_{eff}}} = 3.99$

Taking the ratio of the time periods:

$\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = \left( \dfrac{g}{g_{eff}} \right)^{1/2} = \left( 1 + \dfrac{a^2}{g^2} \right)^{-1/4}$

Since the change in time period is very small, $a$ is small compared to $g$. Using the binomial approximation $(1 + x)^n \approx 1 + nx$:

$\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} \approx 1 - \dfrac{1}{4} \dfrac{a^2}{g^2}$

Substituting the given values $T_1 = 4$ and $T_2 = 3.99$:

$\dfrac{3.99}{4} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{4} \dfrac{a^2}{g^2}$

$\dfrac{1}{4} \dfrac{a^2}{g^2} = 1 - \dfrac{3.99}{4}$

$\dfrac{1}{4} \dfrac{a^2}{g^2} = \dfrac{0.01}{4}$

$\dfrac{a^2}{g^2} = 0.01 = \dfrac{1}{100}$

Taking the square root on both sides:

$\dfrac{a}{g} = \dfrac{1}{10}$

$a = \dfrac{g}{10}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A simple pendulum of length $l$ and mass $m$ is suspended from the ceiling of a car travelling with a speed $v$ on a circular horizontal road of radius $r$. Determine the tension in the string when it is at rest with respect to the car.
questions.solution:
In the frame of reference of the car, the forces acting on the pendulum bob are the gravitational force $mg$ acting vertically downwards, the centrifugal force $\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$ acting horizontally outwards, and the tension $T$ in the string.

Since the pendulum is at rest with respect to the car, it is in equilibrium in the car's frame. The tension $T$ in the string must balance the resultant of the gravitational force and the centrifugal force.

As the gravitational force and the centrifugal force are perpendicular to each other, their resultant is given by:

$F_{res} = \sqrt{(mg)^2 + \left(\dfrac{mv^2}{r}\right)^2}$

Therefore, the tension in the string is:

$T = m \left( g^2 + \dfrac{v^4}{r^2} \right)^{1/2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A simple pendulum of length $l$ is suspended from the ceiling of a car travelling with a speed $v$ on a circular horizontal road of radius $r$. Determine the time period of small oscillations.
questions.solution:
In the frame of the car, the pendulum bob experiences a pseudo force (centrifugal force) in the horizontal direction due to the circular motion of the car.

The centrifugal acceleration is $a_c = \dfrac{v^2}{r}$ directed radially outward.

The acceleration due to gravity $g$ acts vertically downward.

Since the horizontal and vertical accelerations are perpendicular to each other, the effective acceleration due to gravity $g_{eff}$ is given by:

$g_{eff} = \sqrt{g^2 + a_c^2} = \sqrt{g^2 + \left(\dfrac{v^2}{r}\right)^2} = \left( g^2 + \dfrac{v^4}{r^2} \right)^{1/2}$

The time period of small oscillations of a simple pendulum is given by:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g_{eff}}}$

Substituting the value of $g_{eff}$, we get:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{\left( g^2 + \dfrac{v^4}{r^2} \right)^{1/2}}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: As illustrated in the figure, a lady wears an ear-ring suspended by a light wire of length $3 \text{ cm}$. Determine the time period of small oscillations of the ear-ring when the lady is standing on the ground.
questions.solution:
The ear-ring suspended by a light wire can be considered as a simple pendulum.

The time period $T$ of small oscillations for a simple pendulum is given by:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}$

Given:
Length of the wire, $L = 3 \text{ cm} = 0.03 \text{ m}$
Acceleration due to gravity, $g \approx 10 \text{ m/s}^2$

Substituting the values into the formula:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{0.03}{10}}$

$T = 2 \times 3.14 \times \sqrt{0.003}$

$T \approx 6.28 \times 0.0547$

$T \approx 0.34 \text{ s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A lady wears an ear-ring suspended by a light wire of length $3 \text{ cm}$. She sits in a merry-go-round that moves at $4 \text{ m/s}$ in a circle of radius $2 \text{ m}$. Determine the time period of small oscillations of the ear-ring.
questions.solution:
The lady is in a rotating frame of reference, so the ear-ring experiences a centrifugal acceleration in addition to gravity.

Centripetal acceleration of the merry-go-round is given by:

$a = \dfrac{v^2}{R} = \dfrac{4^2}{2} = 8 \text{ m/s}^2$

The effective acceleration due to gravity $g_{\text{eff}}$ is the vector sum of the acceleration due to gravity $g$ and the horizontal acceleration $a$:

$g_{\text{eff}} = \sqrt{g^2 + a^2}$

Taking $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$g_{\text{eff}} = \sqrt{10^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{164} \approx 12.8 \text{ m/s}^2$

The time period of small oscillations for a simple pendulum is:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g_{\text{eff}}}}$

Given $l = 3 \text{ cm} = 0.03 \text{ m}$:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{0.03}{12.8}} \approx 2 \times 3.14 \times 0.0484 \approx 0.30 \text{ s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the time period of small oscillations for a metre stick that is suspended from its $20 \text{ cm}$ mark.
questions.solution:
Length of the metre stick, $L = 1 \text{ m}$

Distance of the center of mass from the point of suspension, $d = 50 \text{ cm} - 20 \text{ cm} = 30 \text{ cm} = 0.3 \text{ m}$

Moment of inertia of the metre stick about the point of suspension is given by the parallel axis theorem:

$I = I_{CM} + M d^2 = \dfrac{M L^2}{12} + M d^2$

$I = M \left( \dfrac{1^2}{12} + (0.3)^2 \right) = M \left( \dfrac{1}{12} + \dfrac{9}{100} \right) = M \left( \dfrac{25 + 27}{300} \right) = \dfrac{52 M}{300} = \dfrac{13 M}{75}$

The time period of a physical pendulum is:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{I}{M g d}}$

Substituting the values and taking $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{\dfrac{13 M}{75}}{M \times 10 \times 0.3}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{13}{75 \times 3}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{13}{225}} = \dfrac{2\pi \sqrt{13}}{15}$

$T \approx \dfrac{2 \times 3.14 \times 3.605}{15} \approx 1.51 \text{ s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ring with mass $m$ and radius $r$ is suspended from a point on its periphery. Find the time period of its small oscillations.
questions.solution:
The time period of a physical pendulum is given by $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{I}{mgd}}$, where $I$ is the moment of inertia about the point of suspension and $d$ is the distance from the point of suspension to the center of mass.

For a ring of mass $m$ and radius $r$, the moment of inertia about its center of mass is $I_{cm} = mr^2$.

Using the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about a point on its periphery is $I = I_{cm} + md^2 = mr^2 + mr^2 = 2mr^2$.

The distance from the point of suspension to the center of mass is $d = r$.

Substituting these values into the time period formula, we get $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{2mr^2}{mgr}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{2r}{g}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform square plate of edge length $a$ is suspended from one of its corners. Calculate the time period of small oscillations for this plate.
questions.solution:
The time period of a physical pendulum is given by $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{I}{mgd}}$, where $I$ is the moment of inertia about the axis of suspension and $d$ is the distance from the point of suspension to the center of mass.

For a square plate of edge length $a$ suspended from a corner, the distance to the center of mass is half the diagonal:

$d = \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{2}}$

The moment of inertia of the square plate about an axis passing through its center of mass and perpendicular to its plane is:

$I_{cm} = \dfrac{m(a^2 + a^2)}{12} = \dfrac{ma^2}{6}$

Using the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about the corner is:

$I = I_{cm} + md^2 = \dfrac{ma^2}{6} + m\left(\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 = \dfrac{ma^2}{6} + \dfrac{ma^2}{2} = \dfrac{2ma^2}{3}$

Substituting $I$ and $d$ into the time period formula, we get:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{\dfrac{2ma^2}{3}}{mg\left(\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{2}}\right)}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{2\sqrt{2}a}{3g}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{\sqrt{8}a}{3g}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the time period of small oscillations for a uniform disc of mass $m$ and radius $r$ that is suspended from a point located at a distance $r/2$ from its centre.
questions.solution:
The time period of a physical pendulum is given by $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{I}{mgd}}$, where $I$ is the moment of inertia about the point of suspension and $d$ is the distance of the centre of mass from the point of suspension.

Given $d = \dfrac{r}{2}$.

The moment of inertia of the uniform disc about its centre of mass is $I_{cm} = \dfrac{1}{2}mr^2$.

Using the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about the point of suspension is:

$I = I_{cm} + md^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}mr^2 + m\left(\dfrac{r}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}mr^2 + \dfrac{1}{4}mr^2 = \dfrac{3}{4}mr^2$

Substituting $I$ and $d$ into the formula for the time period:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{\dfrac{3}{4}mr^2}{mg\left(\dfrac{r}{2}\right)}}$

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{3r}{2g}}$

questions.q: A uniform rod of length $l$ is suspended from one end and undergoes small oscillations. Determine the length of a simple pendulum that possesses a time period identical to that of the rod.
questions.solution:
The time period of a physical pendulum is given by $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{I}{mgd}}$, where $I$ is the moment of inertia about the point of suspension and $d$ is the distance of the center of mass from the point of suspension.

For a uniform rod of mass $m$ and length $l$ suspended from one end, the moment of inertia is $I = \dfrac{ml^2}{3}$ and the distance to the center of mass is $d = \dfrac{l}{2}$.

Substituting these values into the time period formula:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{\dfrac{ml^2}{3}}{mg\left(\dfrac{l}{2}\right)}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{2l}{3g}}$

The time period of a simple pendulum of length $L$ is given by $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}$.

Equating the time periods of the physical pendulum and the simple pendulum:

$2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{2l}{3g}}$

Squaring both sides and solving for $L$, we get:

$L = \dfrac{2l}{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform disc of radius $r$ is suspended through a small hole drilled in it. Determine the minimum possible time period of the disc for small oscillations, along with the distance of the hole from the centre required to achieve this minimum time period.
questions.solution:
The time period of a physical pendulum is given by $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{I}{mgd}}$.

For a uniform disc of radius $r$ and mass $m$, the moment of inertia about its center of mass is $I_{cm} = \dfrac{1}{2}mr^2$.

By the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about a pivot at a distance $d$ from the center is $I = I_{cm} + md^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}mr^2 + md^2$.

Substituting $I$ into the time period formula, we get $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}mr^2 + md^2}{mgd}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{\dfrac{r^2}{2d} + d}{g}}$.

To find the minimum time period, the expression $\left(\dfrac{r^2}{2d} + d\right)$ must be minimized.

Differentiating with respect to $d$ and equating to zero:

$\dfrac{d}{dd}\left(\dfrac{r^2}{2d} + d\right) = -\dfrac{r^2}{2d^2} + 1 = 0 \Rightarrow d = \dfrac{r}{\sqrt{2}}$.

Substituting $d = \dfrac{r}{\sqrt{2}}$ into the time period equation gives the minimum time period:

$T_{min} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{\dfrac{r^2}{2(r/\sqrt{2})} + \dfrac{r}{\sqrt{2}}}{g}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{\dfrac{r}{\sqrt{2}} + \dfrac{r}{\sqrt{2}}}{g}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{r\sqrt{2}}{g}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A pendulum is formed by attaching a hollow sphere of radius $2 \text{ cm}$ to a thread of length $18 \text{ cm}$. Determine the time period of oscillation of this pendulum. Also, how does this period compare to the value calculated using the simple pendulum formula?
options: $0.92 \text{ s}$; it is about $1.5\%$ smaller than the simple pendulum value
$0.89 \text{ s}$; it is about $0.3\%$ larger than the simple pendulum value
$0.89 \text{ s}$; it is about $0.3\%$ smaller than the simple pendulum value
$0.92 \text{ s}$; it is about $1.5\%$ larger than the simple pendulum value
questions.solution:
The distance from the pivot to the center of mass of the hollow sphere is $d = L + R = 18 + 2 = 20 \text{ cm} = 0.2 \text{ m}$.

The moment of inertia of the hollow sphere about the pivot is given by the parallel axis theorem:

$I = I_{cm} + md^2 = \dfrac{2}{3}mR^2 + md^2$

The time period of the physical pendulum is:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{I}{mgd}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{\dfrac{2}{3}mR^2 + md^2}{mgd}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{d}{g} \left(1 + \dfrac{2R^2}{3d^2}\right)}$

The time period of a simple pendulum of length $d$ is $T_0 = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{d}{g}}$.

Using the binomial expansion for $R \ll d$, we get:

$T \approx T_0 \left(1 + \dfrac{R^2}{3d^2}\right)$

Substituting $R = 2 \text{ cm}$ and $d = 20 \text{ cm}$:

$\dfrac{R^2}{3d^2} = \dfrac{2^2}{3 \times 20^2} = \dfrac{4}{1200} = \dfrac{1}{300} \approx 0.0033$

Thus, the time period $T$ is larger than $T_0$ by approximately $0.33\%$, which is about $0.3\%$.

Calculating $T_0$ using $g \approx \pi^2 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$T_0 \approx 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{0.2}{\pi^2}} = 2 \sqrt{0.2} \approx 0.894 \text{ s}$

Therefore, the time period is approximately $0.89 \text{ s}$, and it is about $0.3\%$ larger than the simple pendulum value.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Suspended from a nail in a wall, a closed circular wire experiences small oscillations with an amplitude of $2^\circ$ and a time period of $2 \text{ s}$. Calculate the radius of the circular wire. Take $g = \pi^2 \text{ m/s}^2$.
questions.solution:
The time period of small oscillations for a physical pendulum is given by $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{I}{mgd}}$, where $I$ is the moment of inertia about the axis of rotation and $d$ is the distance from the point of suspension to the center of mass.

For a circular wire (ring) of mass $m$ and radius $R$ suspended from a point on its circumference and oscillating in its own plane, the moment of inertia about the point of suspension is:

$I = I_{CM} + mR^2 = mR^2 + mR^2 = 2mR^2$

The distance from the point of suspension to the center of mass is $d = R$.

Substituting these values into the time period formula, we get:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{2mR^2}{mgR}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{2R}{g}}$

Given that $T = 2 \text{ s}$ and $g = \pi^2 \text{ m/s}^2$, we can substitute these into the equation:

$2 = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{2R}{\pi^2}}$

$1 = \pi \dfrac{\sqrt{2R}}{\pi}$

$1 = \sqrt{2R}$

Squaring both sides:

$2R = 1$

$R = 0.5 \text{ m} = 50 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Suspended from a nail in a wall, a closed circular wire experiences small oscillations with an amplitude of $2^\circ$ and a time period of $2 \text{ s}$. Determine the speed of the particle on the wire farthest from the point of suspension as it passes through its mean position. Take $g = \pi^2 \text{ m/s}^2$.
questions.solution:
The time period of a physical pendulum is given by:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{I}{Mgd}}$

For a closed circular wire (ring) of mass $M$ and radius $R$ oscillating in its own plane about a point on its circumference, the moment of inertia is:

$I = I_{cm} + MR^2 = MR^2 + MR^2 = 2MR^2$

The distance of the center of mass from the suspension point is $d = R$. Substituting these into the time period formula:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{2MR^2}{MgR}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{2R}{g}}$

Given $T = 2 \text{ s}$ and $g = \pi^2 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$2 = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{2R}{\pi^2}} \Rightarrow 1 = \sqrt{2R} \Rightarrow 2R = 1 \text{ m}$

The farthest point on the wire from the point of suspension is diametrically opposite, at a distance $L = 2R = 1 \text{ m}$.

The angular frequency of oscillation is:

$\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T} = \dfrac{2\pi}{2} = \pi \text{ rad/s}$

The angular amplitude in radians is:

$\theta_0 = 2^\circ = 2 \times \dfrac{\pi}{180} = \dfrac{\pi}{90} \text{ rad}$

The maximum angular velocity of the pendulum as it passes through the mean position is:

$\Omega_{max} = \omega \theta_0 = \pi \times \dfrac{\pi}{90} = \dfrac{\pi^2}{90} \text{ rad/s}$

The maximum linear speed of the farthest point is:

$v_{max} = L \Omega_{max} = 1 \times \dfrac{\pi^2}{90} = \dfrac{\pi^2}{90} \text{ m/s}$

Converting to cm/s:

$v_{max} = \dfrac{\pi^2}{90} \times 100 = \dfrac{10\pi^2}{9} \text{ cm/s}$

Using $\pi^2 \approx 9.87$:

$v_{max} \approx \dfrac{10 \times 9.87}{9} \approx 10.96 \text{ cm/s} \approx 11 \text{ cm/s}$

Answer: $11 \text{ cm/s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Suspended from a nail in a wall, a closed circular wire experiences small oscillations with an amplitude of $2^\circ$ and a time period of $2 \text{ s}$. Evaluate the acceleration of the particle on the wire farthest from the point of suspension as it passes through its mean position. Take $g = \pi^2 \text{ m/s}^2$.
options: $3.6 \text{ cm/s}^2$ away from the point of suspension
$1.2 \text{ cm/s}^2$ towards the point of suspension
$1.2 \text{ cm/s}^2$ away from the point of suspension
$2.4 \text{ cm/s}^2$ towards the point of suspension
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of the closed circular wire (ring) about the point of suspension on its circumference is $I = I_{cm} + M R^2 = 2 M R^2$.

The distance of the center of mass from the point of suspension is $d = R$.

The time period of the physical pendulum is given by:

$T = 2 \pi \sqrt{\dfrac{I}{M g d}} = 2 \pi \sqrt{\dfrac{2 M R^2}{M g R}} = 2 \pi \sqrt{\dfrac{2 R}{g}}$

Given $T = 2 \text{ s}$ and $g = \pi^2 \text{ m/s}^2$, we have:

$2 = 2 \pi \sqrt{\dfrac{2 R}{\pi^2}} \Rightarrow 1 = \sqrt{2 R} \Rightarrow 2 R = 1 \text{ m}$

The distance of the farthest point on the wire from the point of suspension is $L = 2 R = 1 \text{ m}$.

The amplitude of oscillation is $\theta_0 = 2^\circ = 2 \times \dfrac{\pi}{180} = \dfrac{\pi}{90} \text{ rad}$.

The angular frequency of the pendulum is $\omega = \dfrac{2 \pi}{T} = \pi \text{ rad/s}$.

The maximum angular velocity of the pendulum as it passes through the mean position is $\Omega = \theta_0 \omega = \dfrac{\pi^2}{90} \text{ rad/s}$.

At the mean position, the angular acceleration is zero, so the tangential acceleration is zero. The acceleration of the farthest point is purely centripetal:

$a = \Omega^2 L = \left( \dfrac{\pi^2}{90} \right)^2 \times 1 = \dfrac{\pi^4}{8100} \text{ m/s}^2$

Converting to $\text{cm/s}^2$:

$a = \dfrac{\pi^4}{81} \text{ cm/s}^2$

Using $\pi^2 \approx 9.87$, we get $\pi^4 \approx 97.4$.

$a \approx \dfrac{97.4}{81} \approx 1.2 \text{ cm/s}^2$

The direction of this centripetal acceleration is towards the center of its circular path, which is the point of suspension.

Answer: $1.2 \text{ cm/s}^2$ towards the point of suspension

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Suspended from a nail in a wall, a closed circular wire experiences small oscillations with an amplitude of $2^\circ$ and a time period of $2 \text{ s}$. Compute the acceleration of the particle on the wire farthest from the point of suspension when it is at an extreme position. Take $g = \pi^2 \text{ m/s}^2$.
options: $34 \text{ cm/s}^2$ away from the mean position
questions.solution:
For a closed circular wire (ring) of radius $R$ suspended from a point on its circumference and oscillating in its own plane, the moment of inertia about the point of suspension is $I = mR^2 + mR^2 = 2mR^2$.

The distance from the point of suspension to the center of mass is $d = R$.

The time period of this physical pendulum is given by:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{I}{mgd}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{2mR^2}{mgR}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{2R}{g}}$

Given $T = 2 \text{ s}$ and $g = \pi^2 \text{ m/s}^2$, substituting these values yields:

$2 = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{2R}{\pi^2}}$

$1 = \sqrt{2R} \Rightarrow 2R = 1 \text{ m}$

The farthest point on the wire from the point of suspension is at a distance $L = 2R = 1 \text{ m}$.

The angular frequency of oscillation is $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T} = \pi \text{ rad/s}$.

The angular amplitude is $\theta_0 = 2^\circ = 2 \times \dfrac{\pi}{180} = \dfrac{\pi}{90} \text{ rad}$.

At the extreme position, the angular velocity is zero, so the radial (centripetal) acceleration is zero. The acceleration is purely tangential.

The maximum angular acceleration at the extreme position is $\alpha = \omega^2 \theta_0$.

The linear acceleration of the farthest point is:

$a = L \alpha = L \omega^2 \theta_0$

Substituting the values:

$a = 1 \times \pi^2 \times \dfrac{\pi}{90} = \dfrac{\pi^3}{90} \text{ m/s}^2$

Converting to $\text{cm/s}^2$:

$a = \dfrac{100 \pi^3}{90} \text{ cm/s}^2 = \dfrac{10 \pi^3}{9} \text{ cm/s}^2$

Using $\pi \approx 3.14$, $\pi^3 \approx 31.0$:

$a \approx \dfrac{10 \times 31.0}{9} \approx 34.4 \text{ cm/s}^2 \approx 34 \text{ cm/s}^2$

In simple harmonic motion, the acceleration is always directed towards the mean position.

Answer: $34 \text{ cm/s}^2$ towards the mean position

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform disc having mass $m$ and radius $r$ is suspended by a wire attached to its centre. If the time period of torsional oscillations is $T$, determine the torsional constant of the wire.
questions.solution:
The time period of torsional oscillations is given by:

$T = 2 \pi \sqrt{\dfrac{I}{C}}$

where $I$ is the moment of inertia of the disc and $C$ is the torsional constant of the wire.

The moment of inertia of a uniform disc about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its plane is:

$I = \dfrac{m r^2}{2}$

Substituting the value of $I$ in the expression for $T$:

$T = 2 \pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m r^2}{2 C}}$

Squaring both sides:

$T^2 = 4 \pi^2 \left( \dfrac{m r^2}{2 C} \right)$

$T^2 = \dfrac{2 \pi^2 m r^2}{C}$

Rearranging for $C$:

$C = \dfrac{2 \pi^2 m r^2}{T^2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two small balls, each having a mass $m$, are joined by a light rigid rod of length $L$. This system is suspended from its centre using a thin wire with a torsional constant $k$. The rod is turned about the wire by an angle $ heta_0$ and released. Determine the force exerted by the rod on one of the balls as the system crosses the mean position.
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of the system about the suspension wire is given by the sum of the moments of inertia of the two balls.

$I = m \left(\dfrac{L}{2}\right)^2 + m \left(\dfrac{L}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{mL^2}{2}$

By the principle of conservation of mechanical energy, the maximum potential energy stored in the torsional wire is converted into kinetic energy as the system crosses the mean position.

$\dfrac{1}{2} k \theta_0^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} I \omega^2$

Substituting the value of $I$:

$k \theta_0^2 = \left(\dfrac{mL^2}{2}\right) \omega^2$

$\omega^2 = \dfrac{2k \theta_0^2}{mL^2}$

As the system crosses the mean position, the ball experiences two forces exerted by the rod: a vertical force to balance its weight and a horizontal force to provide the necessary centripetal acceleration.

The vertical component of the force is $F_y = mg$.

The horizontal component of the force is the centripetal force $F_x = m \omega^2 r$, where $r = \dfrac{L}{2}$.

$F_x = m \left(\dfrac{2k \theta_0^2}{mL^2}\right) \left(\dfrac{L}{2}\right) = \dfrac{k \theta_0^2}{L}$

The net force exerted by the rod on one of the balls is the resultant of these two mutually perpendicular components.

$F = \sqrt{F_x^2 + F_y^2}$

$F = \left[ \left(\dfrac{k \theta_0^2}{L}\right)^2 + (mg)^2 \right]^{1/2}$

$F = \left[ \dfrac{k^2 \theta_0^4}{L^2} + m^2 g^2 \right]^{1/2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle is subjected to two simple harmonic motions of the same time period in the same direction. The amplitude of the first motion is $3.0 \text{ cm}$ while that of the second is $4.0 \text{ cm}$. Determine the resultant amplitude if the phase difference between the motions is $0^\circ$.
questions.solution:
The resultant amplitude $A$ of two simple harmonic motions in the same direction is given by

$A = \sqrt{A_1^2 + A_2^2 + 2A_1A_2 \cos \phi}$

Given $A_1 = 3.0 \text{ cm}$, $A_2 = 4.0 \text{ cm}$, and phase difference $\phi = 0^\circ$.

Substituting the values:

$A = \sqrt{3.0^2 + 4.0^2 + 2(3.0)(4.0) \cos 0^\circ}$

$A = \sqrt{9.0 + 16.0 + 24.0(1)}$

$A = \sqrt{49.0} = 7.0 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle is subjected to two simple harmonic motions of the same time period in the same direction. The amplitude of the first motion is $3.0 \text{ cm}$ while that of the second is $4.0 \text{ cm}$. Determine the resultant amplitude if the phase difference between the motions is $60^\circ$.
questions.solution:
The resultant amplitude $A$ of two simple harmonic motions in the same direction is given by the formula:

$A = \sqrt{A_1^2 + A_2^2 + 2A_1A_2\cos\phi}$

Substituting the given values $A_1 = 3.0 \text{ cm}$, $A_2 = 4.0 \text{ cm}$, and $\phi = 60^\circ$:

$A = \sqrt{3.0^2 + 4.0^2 + 2(3.0)(4.0)\cos 60^\circ}$

$A = \sqrt{9 + 16 + 24 \times \dfrac{1}{2}}$

$A = \sqrt{25 + 12}$

$A = \sqrt{37} \approx 6.08 \text{ cm}$

Rounding to one decimal place, we get $6.1 \text{ cm}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle is subjected to two simple harmonic motions of the same time period in the same direction. The amplitude of the first motion is $3.0 \text{ cm}$ while that of the second is $4.0 \text{ cm}$. Determine the resultant amplitude if the phase difference between the motions is $90^\circ$.
questions.solution:
The resultant amplitude $A$ of two simple harmonic motions of amplitudes $A_1$ and $A_2$ with a phase difference $\phi$ is given by:

$A = \sqrt{A_1^2 + A_2^2 + 2A_1A_2 \cos \phi}$

Given $A_1 = 3.0 \text{ cm}$, $A_2 = 4.0 \text{ cm}$, and $\phi = 90^\circ$.

Substituting the values:

$A = \sqrt{(3.0)^2 + (4.0)^2 + 2(3.0)(4.0) \cos 90^\circ}$

Since $\cos 90^\circ = 0$, we get:

$A = \sqrt{9.0 + 16.0}$

$A = \sqrt{25.0} = 5.0 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three simple harmonic motions with equal amplitudes $A$ and identical time periods in the same direction are combined. The second motion has a phase $60^\circ$ ahead of the first, while the third motion has a phase $60^\circ$ ahead of the second. Determine the amplitude of the resultant motion.
questions.solution:
The three simple harmonic motions can be represented as phasors of length $A$ with angles $0^{\circ}$, $60^{\circ}$, and $120^{\circ}$ respectively.

The resultant amplitude $R$ can be found by resolving the phasors into horizontal and vertical components.

$R_x = A \cos(0^{\circ}) + A \cos(60^{\circ}) + A \cos(120^{\circ})$

$R_x = A \left(1 + \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2}\right) = A$

$R_y = A \sin(0^{\circ}) + A \sin(60^{\circ}) + A \sin(120^{\circ})$

$R_y = A \left(0 + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = \sqrt{3}A$

The resultant amplitude is given by $R = \sqrt{R_x^2 + R_y^2}$

$R = \sqrt{A^2 + (\sqrt{3}A)^2} = \sqrt{A^2 + 3A^2} = \sqrt{4A^2} = 2A$

Alternatively, the resultant of the first and third phasors ($0^{\circ}$ and $120^{\circ}$) has a magnitude of $\sqrt{A^2 + A^2 + 2A^2 \cos(120^{\circ})} = A$ and bisects the angle, directing it at $60^{\circ}$. Since the second phasor is also directed at $60^{\circ}$, their magnitudes add up directly to give $A + A = 2A$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle undergoes two simple harmonic motions described by $x_1 = 2.0 \sin 100 \pi t$ and $x_2 = 2.0 \sin(120 \pi t + \pi/3)$, with $x$ in centimeter and $t$ in second. Determine the displacement of the particle at $t = 0.0125$.
questions.solution:
The total displacement of the particle is given by the principle of superposition:

$x = x_1 + x_2$

Substituting $t = 0.0125$ into the equation for $x_1$:

$x_1 = 2.0 \sin(100 \pi \times 0.0125)$

$x_1 = 2.0 \sin(1.25 \pi) = 2.0 \sin\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{4}\right)$

$x_1 = 2.0 \times \left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = -\sqrt{2} \approx -1.414 \text{ cm}$

Substituting $t = 0.0125$ into the equation for $x_2$:

$x_2 = 2.0 \sin\left(120 \pi \times 0.0125 + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$

$x_2 = 2.0 \sin\left(1.5 \pi + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 2.0 \sin\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2} + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$

Using the trigonometric identity $\sin\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2} + \theta\right) = -\cos \theta$:

$x_2 = -2.0 \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = -2.0 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = -1.0 \text{ cm}$

The total displacement at $t = 0.0125$ is:

$x = x_1 + x_2 = -1.414 - 1.0 = -2.414 \text{ cm}$

Rounding to two decimal places, the displacement is $-2.41 \text{ cm}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle undergoes two simple harmonic motions described by $x_1 = 2.0 \sin 100 \pi t$ and $x_2 = 2.0 \sin(120 \pi t + \pi/3)$, with $x$ in centimeter and $t$ in second. Determine the displacement of the particle at $t = 0.025$.
questions.solution:
The total displacement of the particle is given by the principle of superposition:

$x = x_1 + x_2$

Substituting $t = 0.025$ s into the equations for $x_1$ and $x_2$:

$x_1 = 2.0 \sin(100 \pi \times 0.025) = 2.0 \sin(2.5 \pi)$

$x_1 = 2.0 \sin\left(2\pi + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 2.0 \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 2.0 \times 1 = 2.0 \text{ cm}$

$x_2 = 2.0 \sin\left(120 \pi \times 0.025 + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 2.0 \sin\left(3\pi + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$

$x_2 = 2.0 \left(-\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = -2.0 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = -\sqrt{3} \approx -1.732 \text{ cm}$

The net displacement at $t = 0.025$ s is:

$x = 2.0 - 1.732 = 0.268 \text{ cm} \approx 0.27 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A particle undergoes two simple harmonic motions, one along the X-axis and the other along a line at an angle of $45^\circ$ to the X-axis. These motions are described by
$x = x_0 \sin\omega t$ and $s = s_0 \sin\omega t$.
Determine the amplitude of the resultant motion.
questions.solution:
The two simple harmonic motions are given by $\vec{x} = x_0 \sin\omega t \, \hat{i}$ and $\vec{s} = s_0 \sin\omega t (\cos 45^\circ \hat{i} + \sin 45^\circ \hat{j})$.

Since both simple harmonic motions are in the same phase, the resultant amplitude is the vector sum of their individual amplitudes.

The angle between the two amplitude vectors is $\theta = 45^\circ$.

Using the vector addition formula, the resultant amplitude $A$ is given by:

$A = \sqrt{x_0^2 + s_0^2 + 2 x_0 s_0 \cos 45^\circ}$

$A = \sqrt{x_0^2 + s_0^2 + 2 x_0 s_0 \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)}$

$A = \left[ x_0^2 + s_0^2 + \sqrt{2} x_0 s_0 \right]^{1/2}$
